Retardation sets a time scale for every circuit. The eighth exercise compares it with the period of a signal. The retardation is the new ingredient.

::: {#exr-emw-ret-numbers}
#### When retardation matters

A circuit of size $30\,$cm carries signals of $50\,$Hz, $100\,$MHz and $10\,$GHz. Compare the light-crossing time with the period in each
case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The crossing time is $1\,$ns. The periods are $20\,$ms, $10\,$ns and $0.1\,$ns: retardation is negligible at $50\,$Hz, a $10\%$ effect at
$100\,$MHz, and dominant at $10\,$GHz, where the circuit radiates and behaves as a wave guide (@exm-emm-quasistatic).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The difference between the retarded and the advanced potentials is a source-free field. The ninth exercise proves it. The retardation is the new ingredient.

::: {#exr-emw-ret-advanced}
#### Retarded minus advanced

Show that $G_{\text{ret}} - G_{\text{adv}} = \frac{\delta(t - r) - \delta(t + r)}{4\pi r}$ solves the homogeneous wave equation, and that the difference
of the two potentials of the same sources is a vacuum solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both Green's functions satisfy $\Box G = \delta(t)\delta^3(\mathbf x)$, so their difference has $\Box(G_{\text{ret}} - G_{\text{adv}}) = 0$, and
convolving with the sources gives potentials with $\Box\phi = 0$, $\Box\mathbf A = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A current that varies slowly produces fields close to the static ones, with corrections of order of the retardation. The last
exercise estimates the electric field near a wire with an alternating current.

::: {#exr-emw-ret-ac-wire}
#### The induced field near an AC wire

For $I = I_0\cos\omega t$ in a long wire, the quasi-static vector potential is $A_z \approx -\frac{I}{2\pi}\ln\frac s{s_0}$. Find the induced
$E_z$, and explain why the constant $s_0$ must be fixed by the retarded potential at $s_0 \sim 1/\omega$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$E_z = -\partial_tA_z = -\frac{\omega I_0\sin\omega t}{2\pi}\ln\frac s{s_0}$. The logarithm diverges for an infinite wire; retardation cuts off the
contributions of the wire beyond a distance of order the wavelength, which replaces $s_0$ by about $1/\omega$ ($c/\omega$ in SI units).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Fields of moving charges

The retarded potentials of a point charge can be computed exactly for any motion. The result, the Liénard-Wiechert
potentials, shows a factor that depends on the velocity at the retarded time, and its derivatives separate the field into a
part that follows the charge and a part that leaves it as radiation.

![Left, the field strength $4\pi R_p^2|\mathbf E|/q$ of a charge moving with constant velocity along $\mathbf e_x$, as a polar diagram around
its present position, for $v = 0$, $0.6$ and $0.9$: the field points away from the present position and is compressed toward the plane
perpendicular to the motion, enhanced by $\gamma$ across it and reduced by $1/\gamma^2$ along it. Right, the same function $(1 - v^2)/(1 -
v^2\sin^2\psi)^{3/2}$ against the angle $\psi$ from the velocity (log scale). Generated by
`figures/emw_moving_charge.sage`.](figures/emw_moving_charge.svg){#fig-emw-moving-charge width=95%}

The proposition gives the potentials and the fields of a point charge on an arbitrary trajectory with speed below that of
light. All quantities on the right are evaluated at the retarded time.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emw-lienard-wiechert}
#### Liénard-Wiechert fields

Let a charge $q$ move on $\mathbf r(t)$ with $|\dot{\mathbf r}| < 1$. For each field point $(t, \mathbf x)$ the equation $t - t_r = |\mathbf x - \mathbf
r(t_r)|$ has a unique solution $t_r$; set $\mathbf R = \mathbf x - \mathbf r(t_r)$, $\hat{\mathbf n} = \mathbf R/R$, $\mathbf v = \dot{\mathbf r}(t_r)$, $\mathbf a =
\ddot{\mathbf r}(t_r)$ and $\kappa = 1 - \hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf v$. The retarded potentials are the **Liénard-Wiechert potentials**
$$
\phi = \frac{q}{4\pi\kappa R}, \qquad \mathbf A = \frac{q\mathbf v}{4\pi\kappa R} ,
$$ {#eq-emw-lw-potentials}
and the fields are $\mathbf B = \hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$ with
$$
\mathbf E = \frac{q}{4\pi}\left[\frac{(\hat{\mathbf n} - \mathbf v)(1 - v^2)}{\kappa^3R^2} + \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times\bigl((\hat{\mathbf n} - \mathbf v)\times\mathbf
a\bigr)}{\kappa^3R}\right] ,
$$ {#eq-emw-lw-fields}
the sum of a **velocity field**, falling as $1/R^2$, and an **acceleration field**, falling as $1/R$ and perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf n}$.
*Proof.* Uniqueness: $f(t_r) = t - t_r - |\mathbf x - \mathbf r(t_r)|$ decreases strictly since $|\dot{\mathbf r}| < 1$. In @eq-emw-retarded with $\rho
= q\delta^3(\mathbf x' - \mathbf r(t'))$, write $\rho(t_r)$ as $\int\delta(t' - t + |\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|)\rho(t', \mathbf x')dt'$; integrating over $\mathbf x'$
and then over $t'$ gives the Jacobian $1/\kappa$ of $t' \mapsto t' - t + |\mathbf x - \mathbf r(t')|$. The fields follow by differentiating with
$\partial t_r/\partial t = 1/\kappa$ and $\nabla t_r = -\hat{\mathbf n}/\kappa$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 10.2-10.4;
@pierrus2018solved, Questions 8.12-8.14].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A charge at rest is the first check. The potentials reduce to the Coulomb potential. The general formula contains this case.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-rest}
#### A charge at rest

For $\mathbf v = 0$ and $\mathbf a = 0$, $\kappa = 1$, $\phi = q/4\pi R$, $\mathbf A = 0$, and @eq-emw-lw-fields gives $\mathbf E = q\hat{\mathbf n}/4\pi R^2$, the
field of @exm-ems-point-charge, with $\mathbf B = 0$.
:::

A charge in uniform motion has a field that points from its present position. The retarded quantities combine into the
present ones.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-uniform}
#### A charge in uniform motion

For $\mathbf r = \mathbf vt$, the identity $\kappa R = \sqrt{(\mathbf R_p\cdot\hat{\mathbf v})^2 + (1 - v^2)|\mathbf R_p\times\hat{\mathbf v}|^2}$, with $\mathbf R_p = \mathbf x -
\mathbf vt$ the vector from the present position, turns @eq-emw-lw-fields into $\mathbf E = \frac{q}{4\pi}\frac{(1 - v^2)\mathbf R_p}{R_p^3(1 -
v^2\sin^2\psi)^{3/2}}$, with $\psi$ the angle between $\mathbf R_p$ and $\mathbf v$, and $\mathbf B = \mathbf v\times\mathbf E$ (@fig-emw-moving-charge)
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 10.3; @pierrus2018solved, Question 8.15].
:::

The factor $1/\kappa$ makes an approaching charge's potential larger. It is a geometric effect of the retarded time, not a
change of charge.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-kappa}
#### The factor $\kappa$

A charge approaching the observer ($\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf v > 0$) has $\kappa < 1$: its signal is emitted over a shorter interval of retarded
time than it takes to pass the observer's sphere, and the potential is enhanced by $1/\kappa$; receding charges are weakened.
The total charge is unchanged, since $\int\rho\,d^3x$ is evaluated at a common time, not along the light cone.
:::

The two parts of the field behave differently far away. Only the acceleration field carries energy to infinity. The general formula contains this case.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-two-parts}
#### Velocity field and acceleration field

The velocity field, $\propto R^{-2}$, gives a Poynting flux $\propto R^{-4}$ through a sphere of area $\propto R^2$, which vanishes at large
$R$; the acceleration field gives $|\mathbf E|^2R^2 \propto$ const: a charge radiates if and only if it accelerates, in the sense that energy
crosses arbitrarily large spheres [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 10.4].
:::

The acceleration field is transverse. Together with $\mathbf B = \hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$ it has the structure of a plane wave locally.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-transverse}
#### The radiation field is transverse

$\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\bigl(\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\dots)\bigr) = 0$, so the acceleration field is perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf n}$, and $\mathbf B =
\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$ has the same magnitude and is perpendicular to both: the radiation field is locally the plane wave of
@exm-emw-pw-spherical with $\hat{\mathbf k} = \hat{\mathbf n}$, and $\mathbf S = |\mathbf E|^2\hat{\mathbf n}$.
:::

At low velocity the acceleration field becomes simple. It is the field used in Larmor's formula. The general formula contains this case.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-slow}
#### The radiation field of a slow charge

For $v \ll 1$, $\kappa \approx 1$ and the acceleration field is $\mathbf E_{\text{rad}} = \frac{q}{4\pi R}\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf a)$, of
magnitude $\frac{qa\sin\theta}{4\pi R}$ with $\theta$ the angle between $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf a$, in the plane of $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf a$
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 10.5].
:::

A charge that stops abruptly leaves a shell of radiation. Inside the shell the field is that of the charge at rest, outside that
of the charge still moving.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-stop}
#### A charge that stops

A charge moving uniformly stops in a short time $\tau$ at $t = 0$. At time $t$ the field inside the sphere of radius $t$ around the
stopping point is the Coulomb field of the charge at rest, outside it is the field of the uniform motion continued, and in the
shell of thickness $\tau$ the field lines join with a transverse kink: the acceleration field of @eq-emw-lw-fields, the origin of
bremsstrahlung.
:::

A charge on a circle at relativistic speed emits in a narrow cone along its velocity. The factor $\kappa^{-3}$ produces the
beaming.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-beaming}
#### Beaming of synchrotron radiation

For $v \to 1$, $\kappa = 1 - v\cos\alpha$, with $\alpha$ the angle between $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf v$, is about $\frac{1}{2\gamma^2} + \frac{\alpha^2}2$ for small
$\alpha$, so the fields are enhanced by $\kappa^{-3} \sim \gamma^6$ within a cone of half-angle $\sim1/\gamma$ around $\mathbf v$: an observer sees short
flashes as the cone sweeps past, which is synchrotron light [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 10.6].
:::

The potentials of a uniformly moving charge are explicit at the present time. They also follow from those of a charge at
rest by a Lorentz transformation, as the special relativity chapter shows.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-uniform-potential}
#### The potential of a uniformly moving charge

With $\kappa R$ from @exm-emw-lw-uniform, $\phi = \frac{q}{4\pi\sqrt{(x - vt)^2 + (1 - v^2)(y^2 + z^2)}} = \frac{q\gamma}{4\pi\sqrt{\gamma^2(x - vt)^2 + y^2 +
z^2}}$ for $\mathbf v = v\mathbf e_x$, and $\mathbf A = \mathbf v\phi$, with $\gamma = (1 - v^2)^{-1/2}$ [@pierrus2018solved, Question 8.15].
:::

A charge moving slowly on a circle is a rotating dipole seen from far away. Its radiation field follows from the acceleration term.

::: {#exm-emw-lw-circle}
#### A charge on a circle

For $\mathbf r = \rho(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t, 0)$ with $\rho\omega \ll 1$, $\mathbf a = -\omega^2\mathbf r$, and the acceleration field at distance $R \gg \rho$ is
$\frac{q}{4\pi R}\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf a)$, that of the rotating dipole $q\mathbf r(t)$ of @exm-emw-dip-rotating: circularly polarised
along the axis of the orbit [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Problem 10.2].
:::

Both hold identically for $(x, y, z) \neq (vt, 0, 0)$:

The retarded time of a uniformly moving charge solves a quadratic equation. The second exercise solves it with Sage. The general formula contains this case.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-retarded-time}
#### The retarded time of uniform motion

For $\mathbf r(t) = vt\,\mathbf e_x$, solve $t - t_r = |\mathbf x - vt_r\mathbf e_x|$ for $t_r$ with Sage, choose the root with $t_r < t$, and evaluate $\kappa R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t_r = \gamma^2\bigl(t - vx - \sqrt{(x - vt)^2 + (1 - v^2)(y^2 + z^2)}\bigr)$, and $\kappa R = \sqrt{(x - vt)^2 + (1 - v^2)(y^2 + z^2)}$:

{{< sage exr-emw-lw-retarded-time >}}
:::

The field of uniform motion can be computed from the potentials at the present time. The third exercise does it with Sage.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-field-uniform}
#### The field of uniform motion from the potentials

With Sage, compute $\mathbf E = -\nabla\phi - \partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B = \nabla\times\mathbf A$ from @exm-emw-lw-uniform-potential, and compare with the
formula of @exm-emw-lw-uniform.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbf E = \frac{q\gamma(x - vt, y, z)}{4\pi(\gamma^2(x - vt)^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}$, which is the stated formula, and $\mathbf B = \mathbf v\times\mathbf E$:

{{< sage exr-emw-lw-field-uniform >}}
:::

The field of a fast charge is concentrated in the transverse plane. The fourth exercise compares its strength along and across
the motion.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-flattening}
#### Along and across the motion

At a given distance $R_p$ from the present position, find the ratio of $|\mathbf E|$ across the motion to $|\mathbf E|$ along it, and the angular
width of the region where the field exceeds half its maximum, for $\gamma \gg 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Across, $(1 - v^2)(1 - v^2)^{-3/2} = \gamma$; along, $1 - v^2 = \gamma^{-2}$; ratio $\gamma^3$. Near $\psi = \pi/2$, $1 - v^2\sin^2\psi \approx \gamma^{-2} +
(\psi - \frac\pi2)^2$, so the field halves when $(\psi - \frac\pi2)^2\gamma^2 = 2^{2/3} - 1$, a width of order $1/\gamma$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The magnetic field of a moving charge is perpendicular to the line from the retarded position. The fifth exercise checks
this against the uniform-motion formula.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-b}
#### $\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf v\times\mathbf E$ for uniform motion

For uniform motion the magnetic field is $\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$ by @prp-emw-lienard-wiechert, with $\hat{\mathbf n}$ from the retarded position,
and $\mathbf v\times\mathbf E$ by @exm-emw-lw-uniform. Show that the two agree.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\mathbf a = 0$, $\mathbf E$ is parallel to $\hat{\mathbf n} - \mathbf v$, and $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n} - \mathbf v) = -\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf v = \mathbf v\times\hat{\mathbf n}
= \mathbf v\times(\hat{\mathbf n} - \mathbf v)$. So $\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E = \mathbf v\times\mathbf E$, although $\hat{\mathbf n}$ points from the retarded position and
$\mathbf E$ along the line from the present one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The acceleration field is orthogonal to the direction of observation. The sixth exercise checks it and computes its magnitude
for an acceleration along the velocity.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-acceleration}
#### The acceleration field

Show that the second term of @eq-emw-lw-fields is perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf n}$, and that for $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$ its magnitude is
$\frac{qa\sin\alpha}{4\pi\kappa^3R}$, with $\alpha$ the angle between $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf v$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
It is a cross product with $\hat{\mathbf n}$. For $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$, $(\hat{\mathbf n} - \mathbf v)\times\mathbf a = \hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf a$, and $|\hat{\mathbf
n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf a)| = a\sin\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

An electron of $1\,$GeV passes at distance $b = 1\,$cm. With Sage, find $\gamma$, the peak transverse field $\gamma e/4\pi\varepsilon_0b^2$, and the
duration $b/\gamma c$ of the pulse.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma = 1957$, the peak field is $28\,$mV/m, and the pulse lasts $1.7\times10^{-14}\,$s: a flash of virtual photons with frequencies up to

{{< sage exr-emw-lw-pulse >}}

A uniformly moving charge does not radiate. The eighth exercise shows it from the energy flux through a large sphere.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-no-radiation}
#### Uniform motion does not radiate

Using @exm-emw-lw-uniform, show that the Poynting flux through a sphere of radius $R$ around the present position tends to zero as $R \to
\infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\mathbf E| \leq \frac{q\gamma}{4\pi R^2}$ and $|\mathbf B| \leq v|\mathbf E|$, so $|\mathbf S| \leq \frac{q^2\gamma^2}{16\pi^2R^4}$ and the flux through the sphere is
$O(R^{-2})$. The field moves along with the charge without leaving it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The energy carried away by a charge that stops can be estimated from Larmor's formula of the next unit. The ninth exercise
compares it with the kinetic energy.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-stop-energy}
#### Energy lost in stopping

An electron with speed $v \ll c$ stops uniformly in time $\tau$. Using the power $\frac{e^2a^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}$ of @prp-emw-larmor, compare the
radiated energy with $\frac12mv^2$, and evaluate the ratio for $\tau = 10^{-15}\,$s.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The radiated energy is $\frac{e^2v^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3\tau}$, and its ratio to $\frac12mv^2$ is $\frac{e^2}{3\pi\varepsilon_0mc^3\tau} = \frac{4r_e}{3c\tau}$
(@exm-ems-energy-self), $1.3\times10^{-8}$ for $\tau = 10^{-15}\,$s: tiny unless the stopping takes about $10^{-23}\,$s.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The uniqueness of the retarded time requires the speed to stay below that of light. The last exercise shows what goes wrong
otherwise.

::: {#exr-emw-lw-uniqueness}
#### One retarded time

Show that $f(t') = t - t' - |\mathbf x - \mathbf r(t')|$ is strictly decreasing when $|\dot{\mathbf r}| < 1$, positive for $t' \to -\infty$ if the charge
moves slower than light, and zero at exactly one $t' < t$. What happens for a source faster than light?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f'(t') = -1 + \hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\dot{\mathbf r} < 0$. $f(t) = -|\mathbf x - \mathbf r(t)| \leq 0$ and $f \to +\infty$ as $t' \to -\infty$ because $|\mathbf r(t')|$ grows
slower than $|t'|$, so there is exactly one zero. For a superluminal source $f$ can have several zeros: several retarded positions
contribute, as for the shock fronts of Cherenkov radiation in a medium.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Radiation of accelerated charges

The acceleration field of @prp-emw-lienard-wiechert falls as $1/R$, so its energy flux through a large sphere does not
vanish. For a slowly moving charge the flux has a simple angular pattern and a total that depends only on the square of
the acceleration.

![Angular distribution of the power radiated by a charge whose acceleration is parallel to its velocity, $dP/d\Omega$ in
the direction at angle $\theta$ from $\mathbf v$, normalised to its maximum, for $v = 0$ (the Larmor pattern $\sin^2\theta$), $0.5$
and $0.9$: as $v$ grows the lobes tilt forward into a cone of half-angle of order $1/\gamma$. Generated by
`figures/emw_larmor.sage`.](figures/emw_larmor.svg){#fig-emw-larmor width=80%}

The proposition gives the radiated power of a slow charge and its relativistic generalisation. Only the first is proved
here; the second is the Lorentz-invariant form of the first.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emw-larmor}
#### Larmor's formula

A charge $q$ with velocity $v \ll 1$ and acceleration $\mathbf a$ produces at large distance $R$ the radiation field $\mathbf E =
\frac{q}{4\pi R}\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf a)$, $\mathbf B = \hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$, evaluated at the retarded time, and radiates the
power
$$
\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = \frac{q^2a^2}{16\pi^2}\sin^2\theta, \qquad P = \frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi} ,
$$ {#eq-emw-larmor}
with $\theta$ the angle between $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf a$; in SI units $P = \frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}$. For arbitrary
velocity the power is **Liénard's formula** $P = \frac{q^2}{6\pi}\gamma^6\bigl(a^2 - |\mathbf v\times\mathbf a|^2\bigr)$, $\gamma = (1 -
v^2)^{-1/2}$. *Proof.* The field is the slow limit of @eq-emw-lw-fields (@exm-emw-lw-slow). Its Poynting vector is $|\mathbf
E|^2\hat{\mathbf n}$ with $|\mathbf E| = \frac{qa\sin\theta}{4\pi R}$, so $\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = R^2|\mathbf E|^2$, and $\int\sin^2\theta\,d\Omega =
\frac{8\pi}3$. Liénard's formula follows by writing the power as a Lorentz scalar, as the classical field theory chapter does
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 10.5-10.6].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The angular pattern has no radiation along the acceleration. The power is largest at right angles to it. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-pattern}
#### The doughnut pattern

$\sin^2\theta$ vanishes along $\pm\mathbf a$ and is largest in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf a$; the radiation is linearly polarised
in the plane of $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf a$ (@exm-emw-pol-dipole). About $70\%$ of the power goes into $60^\circ < \theta < 120^\circ$
(@fig-emw-larmor, curve $v = 0$).
:::

A charge oscillating harmonically radiates at its frequency. The average power grows as the fourth power of the frequency. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-oscillating}
#### An oscillating charge

For $z(t) = z_0\cos\omega t$, $a = -\omega^2z_0\cos\omega t$ and $\langle P\rangle = \frac{q^2\omega^4z_0^2}{12\pi}$, the dipole power of
@prp-emw-dipole-radiation with $p_0 = qz_0$. Doubling the frequency multiplies the radiated power by $16$.
:::

At high speed the same acceleration radiates much more. Liénard's formula distinguishes accelerations along and across
the velocity. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-lienard}
#### Linear and circular acceleration

For $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$, $P = \frac{q^2}{6\pi}\gamma^6a^2$; for $\mathbf a \perp \mathbf v$, $P = \frac{q^2}{6\pi}\gamma^4a^2$. In terms of the force,
$\dot p = m\gamma^3a$ in the first case and $m\gamma a$ in the second, so $P = \frac{q^2\dot p^2}{6\pi m^2}$ along the velocity and
$\frac{q^2\gamma^2\dot p^2}{6\pi m^2}$ across it [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 10.6.2-10.6.3].
:::

A linear accelerator loses very little to radiation. The loss compared with the energy gain is set by the classical
electron radius.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-linac}
#### Radiation in a linear accelerator

With @exm-emw-larmor-lienard, the ratio of radiated power to the power $v\dot p$ supplied is $\frac{q^2\dot p}{6\pi m^2v}$, which in SI
units is $\frac23\frac{r_e}{mc^2}\frac{d\mathcal E}{dx}$ for an electron with $v \approx c$. For a gradient of $10\,$MeV/m this is $4\times
10^{-14}$: negligible.
:::

In a circular accelerator the loss grows as the fourth power of the energy. It limits electron rings. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-synchrotron}
#### Synchrotron losses

On a circle of radius $\rho$, $a = v^2/\rho$, and the energy lost per turn is $\frac{q^2\gamma^4v^3}{6\pi\rho^2}\cdot\frac{2\pi\rho}v = \frac{q^2\gamma^4v^2}{3\rho}$.
In SI units, for an electron of $100\,$GeV on $\rho = 3.1\,$km, $\frac{e^2\gamma^4}{3\varepsilon_0\rho} = 2.9\,$GeV per turn, while a proton of
the same energy loses $(m_e/m_p)^4 \approx 10^{-13}$ times as much.
:::

An electron circling in a magnetic field radiates at the cyclotron frequency. Its energy decays exponentially. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-cyclotron}
#### Cyclotron radiation

An electron with $v \ll 1$ in a field $B$ has $a = \omega v$, $\omega = eB/m$, so $P = \frac{e^2\omega^2v^2}{6\pi} = \frac{e^2\omega^2}{3\pi m}\mathcal
E$ with $\mathcal E = \frac12mv^2$: the energy decays with time constant $\frac{3\pi m}{e^2\omega^2}$, $2.6\,$s in $1\,$T
(@exr-emw-larmor-cyclotron) [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.1].
:::

A free electron in a light wave oscillates and radiates. The ratio of the scattered power to the incident intensity is the
Thomson cross-section.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-thomson}
#### Thomson scattering

In a wave of amplitude $E_0$ an electron has $a = eE_0\cos\omega t/m$ and radiates $\langle P\rangle = \frac{e^4E_0^2}{12\pi m^2}$. Dividing by the
intensity $\frac12E_0^2$ gives $\sigma_T = \frac{e^4}{6\pi m^2} = \frac{8\pi}3r_e^2 = 6.65\times10^{-29}\,$m$^2$ in SI units, independent of the
frequency [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.9].
:::

At relativistic speed the radiation is thrown forward. The factor $\kappa^{-5}$ in the angular distribution produces the cone. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-beaming}
#### Forward beaming

For $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$, the power per solid angle measured at the charge's retarded time is $\frac{q^2a^2}{16\pi^2}\frac{\sin^2\alpha}{(1 -
v\cos\alpha)^5}$, with $\alpha$ the angle from $\mathbf v$; its maximum moves to $\cos\alpha = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 15v^2} - 1}{3v}$, which for $\gamma \gg 1$
is $\alpha \approx \frac1{2\gamma}$ (@fig-emw-larmor, @exr-emw-larmor-beaming) [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 10.6].
:::

A classical electron on a Bohr orbit radiates its binding energy in a fraction of a nanosecond. Larmor's formula shows why
classical atoms cannot exist.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-atom}
#### The classical atom

At the Bohr radius the electron's acceleration is $a = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0m_ea_0^2} = 9.0\times10^{22}\,$m/s$^2$, and $P = 4.7\times
10^{-8}\,$W; the binding energy $13.6\,$eV would be radiated in about $5\times10^{-11}\,$s, and the orbit collapses in about $10^{-11}\,$s
[@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.2].
:::

The radiated power depends on the charge and the mass only through $q^2/m^2$ for a given force. Heavy particles radiate much
less.

::: {#exm-emw-larmor-mass}
#### Light particles radiate

For a given force $\mathbf F = m\mathbf a$, @eq-emw-larmor gives $P = \frac{q^2F^2}{6\pi m^2}$: an electron radiates $(m_p/m_e)^2 = 3.4\times10^6$ times more
than a proton under the same force, which is why bremsstrahlung and synchrotron light come from electrons.
:::
::::

With Sage, integrate $\frac{q^2a^2}{16\pi^2}\sin^2\theta$ over the sphere, and find the fraction of the power emitted within $30^\circ$ of the

With Sage, solve $\frac{d\mathcal E}{dt} = -\frac{e^2\omega^2}{3\pi m}\mathcal E$ and evaluate the time constant in SI units, $\frac{3\pi\varepsilon_0m^3c^3}{e^4B^2}$,
for an electron in $1\,$T and in $10\,$T [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.1].

$\mathcal E = \mathcal E_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = 2.6\,$s in $1\,$T and $0.026\,$s in $10\,$T:

Two charges on a rotating rod radiate differently depending on their signs. The fourth exercise compares the cases. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exr-emw-larmor-pair}
#### Two charges on a rotating rod

Charges at the two ends of a rod of length $2\ell$ rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ about its centre: compare the radiated power
when they are $+q$, $+q$ and when they are $+q$, $-q$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.4].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The fields add coherently when $\ell\omega \ll 1$, so the power is that of the total dipole $\mathbf p = \sum q_a\mathbf x_a$. For $+q$, $-q$, $\mathbf p$
rotates with $|\mathbf p| = 2q\ell$ and $P = \frac{4q^2\ell^2\omega^4}{6\pi}$; for $+q$, $+q$, $\mathbf p = 0$ and the leading radiation is quadrupole,
smaller by a factor of order $(\ell\omega)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The ratio of radiated to supplied power in a linear accelerator was estimated in @exm-emw-larmor-linac. The fifth exercise
derives it.

::: {#exr-emw-larmor-linac}
#### Losses in a linear accelerator

From $P = \frac{q^2\dot p^2}{6\pi m^2}$ for $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$, show that $\frac{P}{v\dot p} = \frac{q^2\dot p}{6\pi m^2v}$, and that $\dot p = \frac{d\mathcal E}{dx}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The power supplied is $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v = v\dot p$, so the ratio is as stated. Since $d\mathcal E = v\,dp$ (relativistic, @exm-emm-relativistic-work),
$\dot p = \frac{d\mathcal E}{v\,dt} = \frac{d\mathcal E}{dx}$.
:::

$\sigma_T = 6.65\times10^{-29}\,$m$^2$ and the mean free path $1/(n\sigma_T) = 1.5\,$cm:

The forward peak of the relativistic pattern moves with the speed. The seventh exercise locates it with Sage. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exr-emw-larmor-beaming}
#### Where the beam points

With Sage, maximise $\frac{\sin^2\alpha}{(1 - v\cos\alpha)^5}$ over $\alpha$, check $\cos\alpha_{\max} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 15v^2} - 1}{3v}$, and evaluate $\alpha_{\max}$ and
$\frac{1}{2\gamma}$ for $v = 0.9$ and $0.99$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The derivative vanishes at the stated cosine; $\alpha_{\max} = 13.4^\circ$ and $\frac1{2\gamma} = 12.5^\circ$ for $v = 0.9$; $4.1^\circ$ and $4.0^\circ$ for $0.99$:

{{< sage exr-emw-larmor-beaming >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Liénard's formula must reduce to Larmor's at low speed. The eighth exercise checks the limits. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exr-emw-larmor-lienard-limits}
#### Limits of Liénard's formula

Show that Liénard's formula reduces to @eq-emw-larmor for $v \to 0$, gives $\gamma^6a^2$ for $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$ and $\gamma^4a^2$ for $\mathbf
a \perp \mathbf v$, and is never negative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $v \to 0$, $\gamma \to 1$ and $|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a| \to 0$. For $\mathbf a \parallel \mathbf v$, $\mathbf v\times\mathbf a = 0$; for $\mathbf a \perp \mathbf v$, $|\mathbf
v\times\mathbf a|^2 = v^2a^2$ and $\gamma^6(1 - v^2) = \gamma^4$. Since $|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a| \leq va < a$, the bracket is positive.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Light scattered at a right angle is polarised. The ninth exercise explains why. The numbers show how small or large the effect can be.

::: {#exr-emw-larmor-scattered-polarisation}
#### Polarisation of scattered light

Unpolarised light travelling along $\mathbf e_z$ is scattered by free electrons. Show that the light scattered along $\mathbf e_x$ is linearly
polarised along $\mathbf e_y$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.8].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The electrons oscillate in the $xy$ plane, along the incident field. Seen along $\mathbf e_x$, the $x$ component of $\mathbf a$ is along
$\hat{\mathbf n}$ and does not radiate ($\sin\theta = 0$), while the $y$ component gives a field along $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf e_y) =
-\mathbf e_y$: the skylight at $90^\circ$ from the Sun is strongly polarised.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Proton rings are limited by the strength of their magnets, electron rings by radiation. The last exercise compares the losses.

::: {#exr-emw-larmor-proton-ring}
#### Protons and electrons in the same ring

At the same energy $\mathcal E \gg m$ and radius, compare the synchrotron loss per turn of a proton and of an electron, and evaluate it for
the protons of $7\,$TeV in the LHC ($\rho = 2.8\,$km) with the formula of @exm-emw-larmor-synchrotron.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The loss scales as $\gamma^4 = (\mathcal E/m)^4$, so the ratio is $(m_e/m_p)^4 = 8.8\times10^{-14}$. For the LHC, $\gamma = 7460$ and $\frac{e^2\gamma^4}{3\varepsilon_0\rho} =
6.7\,$keV per turn, small but enough to heat the cryogenic beam pipe.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Dipole radiation and the radiation zones

A source whose size is small compared with the wavelength radiates mainly through its electric dipole moment. Its field,
computed at every distance, shows three regions with different behaviour: a near zone where the field is static, a far zone
where it is radiation, and an induction zone between them.

![Fields of a dipole $\mathbf p(t) = p_0\cos(\omega t)\mathbf e_z$ in the equatorial plane, magnitudes of the three terms of the electric field,
$1/(kr)^3$, $1/(kr)^2$ and $1/kr$ in units of $k^3p_0/4\pi$, against $kr$ (log scale): the static $r^{-3}$ term dominates in the near
zone $kr \ll 1$, the radiation term $r^{-1}$ in the far zone $kr \gg 1$, and the three are comparable in the induction zone around $kr =
1$. Right, the time-averaged energy flux, purely radial with the pattern $\sin^2\theta$ at every distance. Generated by
`figures/emw_zones.sage`.](figures/emw_zones.svg){#fig-emw-zones width=95%}

The proposition gives the far field of a small slowly moving source. It reduces Larmor's formula for several charges to one
vector, the second time derivative of the dipole moment.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emw-dipole-radiation}
#### Electric dipole radiation

Let a source of size $d$ have charges moving slowly, so that its dipole moment $\mathbf p(t) = \int\rho\,\mathbf x\,d^3x$ changes on time scales
$T \gg d$. In the far zone $r \gg T$ the fields are
$$
\mathbf E = \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times\bigl(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\ddot{\mathbf p}(t - r)\bigr)}{4\pi r}, \qquad \mathbf B = \frac{\ddot{\mathbf p}(t - r)\times\hat{\mathbf
n}}{4\pi r} ,
$$ {#eq-emw-dipole-field}
and the radiated power is $\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = \frac{|\ddot{\mathbf p}|^2\sin^2\theta}{16\pi^2}$, $P = \frac{|\ddot{\mathbf p}|^2}{6\pi}$, with $\theta$ the angle
from $\ddot{\mathbf p}$; for $\mathbf p = \operatorname{Re}(\mathbf p_0e^{-i\omega t})$, $\langle P\rangle = \frac{\omega^4|\mathbf p_0|^2}{12\pi}$. The next terms are the
**magnetic dipole** radiation, with $\mathbf E \leftrightarrow \mathbf B$ up to sign and $\mathbf p \to \mathbf m$ (@def-ems-magnetic-dipole), $P =
\frac{|\ddot{\mathbf m}|^2}{6\pi}$, and the **electric quadrupole** radiation, $P = \frac{1}{720\pi}\sum_{ij}\dddot Q_{ij}^2$ (@prp-fam-multipole),
both smaller by $(d/T)^2$. *Proof.* By @exm-emw-ret-far, $\mathbf A \approx \frac1{4\pi r}\int\mathbf J(t - r, \mathbf x')d^3x' = \frac{\dot{\mathbf p}(t -
r)}{4\pi r}$, since $\int\mathbf J = \dot{\mathbf p}$ by continuity. In the far zone $\nabla$ acting on $t - r$ gives $-\hat{\mathbf n}\partial_t$, so $\mathbf B
= \nabla\times\mathbf A = -\hat{\mathbf n}\times\partial_t\mathbf A = \frac{\ddot{\mathbf p}\times\hat{\mathbf n}}{4\pi r}$, and $\mathbf E = \mathbf B\times\hat{\mathbf n}$ for the
outgoing wave (@exm-emw-pw-spherical); the power follows as in @prp-emw-larmor [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 11.2-11.2.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
An oscillating dipole radiates a power that grows as the fourth power of the frequency. The example writes the average.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-oscillating}
#### An oscillating dipole

For $\mathbf p = p_0\cos(\omega t)\mathbf e_z$, $|\ddot{\mathbf p}|^2 = \omega^4p_0^2\cos^2\omega t$ and $\langle P\rangle = \frac{\omega^4p_0^2}{12\pi}$, $\frac{\omega^4p_0^2}{12\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}$
in SI units; for a point charge this is @exm-emw-larmor-oscillating [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Problem 10.1].
:::

A rotating dipole is two oscillating dipoles a quarter period apart. It radiates a constant power with circular
polarisation along its axis.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-rotating}
#### A rotating dipole

For $\mathbf p = p_0(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t, 0)$, $|\ddot{\mathbf p}| = \omega^2p_0$ is constant, $P = \frac{\omega^4p_0^2}{6\pi}$, twice the average of one
linear dipole, and $\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = \frac{\omega^4p_0^2}{32\pi^2}(1 + \cos^2\theta)$: circularly polarised along the axis, linearly in the
plane of rotation (@exm-emw-pol-dipole).
:::

A short antenna is an oscillating dipole driven by a current. Its radiated power defines a radiation resistance. The dipole approximation makes the computation short.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-antenna}
#### Radiation resistance of a short antenna

A wire of length $\ell \ll \lambda$ with uniform current $I_0\cos\omega t$ has $\dot p = I\ell$, so $\langle P\rangle = \frac{\omega^2I_0^2\ell^2}{12\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}$
in SI units, which equals $\frac12R_{\text{rad}}I_0^2$ with $R_{\text{rad}} = \frac{2\pi}3Z_0\bigl(\frac\ell\lambda\bigr)^2 \approx 789\,\Omega\bigl(\frac\ell\lambda\bigr)^2$,
$Z_0 = 1/\varepsilon_0c = 377\,\Omega$ [@pierrus2018solved, Question 11.13].
:::

A small current loop radiates through its magnetic dipole moment. Its fields are those of the electric dipole with the roles
of $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ exchanged.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-magnetic}
#### A loop antenna

A loop of radius $b$ with current $I_0\cos\omega t$ has $m = \pi b^2I_0\cos\omega t$ and radiates $\langle P\rangle = \frac{\omega^4\pi^2b^4I_0^2}{12\pi}$; the
far field is $\mathbf B = \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\ddot{\mathbf m})}{4\pi r}$, $\mathbf E = -\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf B$. Compared with an electric dipole of
the same current and size it is weaker by $(\omega b)^2$ [@pierrus2018solved, Question 11.12].
:::

A rotating neutron star with a magnetic dipole tilted from its axis radiates at its rotation frequency. The radiated power
slows it down.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-pulsar}
#### The spin-down of a pulsar

A dipole $\mathbf m$ at angle $\alpha$ to the rotation axis has $|\ddot{\mathbf m}| = \omega^2m\sin\alpha$ and $P = \frac{\omega^4m^2\sin^2\alpha}{6\pi}$. Equating
it to the loss of rotational energy $-I_*\omega\dot\omega$ gives the field of the star from its period and spin-down rate: of order $10^9\,$T for
the Crab pulsar (@exr-emw-dip-pulsar) [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.5].
:::

The $\omega^4$ law explains the colour of the sky. Molecules scatter blue light much more than red. The dipole approximation makes the computation short.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-rayleigh}
#### Why the sky is blue

A molecule in a light wave acquires a dipole $\mathbf p = \alpha\mathbf E$ (with polarisability $\alpha$ independent of frequency far from
resonances), and radiates $\propto\omega^4|\mathbf E|^2$: blue light at $450\,$nm is scattered $(700/450)^4 = 5.9$ times more than red at
$700\,$nm, and the scattered light at $90^\circ$ is polarised (@exr-emw-larmor-scattered-polarisation).
:::

A system of charges with the same charge-to-mass ratio has no dipole radiation. Its dipole moment is tied to its centre of
mass.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-same-ratio}
#### No dipole radiation from like particles

If every charge has $q_a/m_a = \kappa$, then $\mathbf p = \kappa\sum m_a\mathbf x_a = \kappa M\mathbf X$, and for an isolated system $\ddot{\mathbf X} = 0$, so
$\ddot{\mathbf p} = 0$: two electrons colliding radiate only through their quadrupole moment, much more weakly than an electron and a
proton (@exr-emw-dip-same-ratio).
:::

Quadrupole radiation appears when the dipole moment is constant. Its angular pattern has four lobes. The dipole approximation makes the computation short.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-quadrupole}
#### Quadrupole radiation

For the linear quadrupole $Q_{zz} = Q_0\cos\omega t$, $Q_{xx} = Q_{yy} = -\frac12Q_0\cos\omega t$ (charges $\pm$ on the $z$ axis), $\sum\dddot Q_{ij}^2$
averages to $\frac34\omega^6Q_0^2$ and $\langle P\rangle = \frac{\omega^6Q_0^2}{960\pi}$, with the pattern $\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$: no radiation along the axis
or in the equatorial plane [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 11.2.2].
:::

Two dipoles at a distance comparable with the wavelength interfere. The pattern of an array can be steered by the phases.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-array}
#### Two antennas

Two parallel dipoles along $\mathbf e_z$ at $x = \pm\frac d2$, in phase, have far fields with path difference $d\sin\theta\cos\varphi$; the
power pattern is $\sin^2\theta\cos^2\bigl(\frac{kd}2\sin\theta\cos\varphi\bigr)$ times that of one. For $d = \lambda/2$ the radiation along
$\pm\mathbf e_x$ cancels and that along $\pm\mathbf e_y$ doubles in amplitude [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.10].
:::

The polarisation of the dipole field is fixed by the geometry. The example gives its direction. The dipole approximation makes the computation short.

::: {#exm-emw-dip-polarisation}
#### Direction of the radiated field

$\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\ddot{\mathbf p}) = (\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\ddot{\mathbf p})\hat{\mathbf n} - \ddot{\mathbf p}$ is minus the component of $\ddot{\mathbf
p}$ perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf n}$: the electric field lies in the plane of $\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf p$, along the meridian when $\mathbf p
\parallel \mathbf e_z$, and $\mathbf B$ along the parallels.
:::

The far-zone fields follow from the retarded vector potential. The ninth exercise asks for the derivative of a function
of $t - r$.

::: {#exr-emw-dip-derivation}
#### Derivatives of retarded functions

For $\mathbf A = \frac{\mathbf f(t - r)}{4\pi r}$, show that $\nabla\times\mathbf A = -\frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf f'(t - r)}{4\pi r} + O(r^{-2})$, and use it to
derive @eq-emw-dipole-field.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla f_i(t - r) = -f_i'\hat{\mathbf n}$, so $\nabla\times\mathbf f = -\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf f'$, and the derivative of $1/r$ gives $O(r^{-2})$. With $\mathbf f =
\dot{\mathbf p}$, $\mathbf B = -\frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times\ddot{\mathbf p}}{4\pi r} = \frac{\ddot{\mathbf p}\times\hat{\mathbf n}}{4\pi r}$; then $\mathbf E = \mathbf B\times\hat{\mathbf
n} = \frac{(\ddot{\mathbf p}\times\hat{\mathbf n})\times\hat{\mathbf n}}{4\pi r} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\ddot{\mathbf p})}{4\pi r}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

The full field of an oscillating dipole contains three powers of the distance. The definition names the regions where each
dominates.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-emw-radiation-zones}
#### Radiation zones

For a source of size $d$ oscillating at angular frequency $\omega$ with wavelength $\lambda = 2\pi/\omega \gg d$ (SI: $2\pi c/\omega$), the
**near zone** is $d \ll r \ll \lambda$, the **induction zone** $r \sim \lambda$, and the **far zone** or **radiation zone** $r \gg \lambda$. For a
dipole $\mathbf p = \operatorname{Re}(\mathbf p_0e^{-i\omega t})$ at the origin, with $k = \omega$, the fields are the real parts of
$$
\mathbf E = \frac{e^{i(kr - \omega t)}}{4\pi}\Bigl[\frac{k^2(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf p_0)\times\hat{\mathbf n}}r + \bigl(3\hat{\mathbf n}(\hat{\mathbf
n}\cdot\mathbf p_0) - \mathbf p_0\bigr)\Bigl(\frac1{r^3} - \frac{ik}{r^2}\Bigr)\Bigr], \qquad \mathbf B = \frac{k^2e^{i(kr - \omega t)}}{4\pi}(\hat{\mathbf
n}\times\mathbf p_0)\frac1r\Bigl(1 - \frac1{ikr}\Bigr) ;
$$ {#eq-emw-dipole-full}
the terms in $r^{-3}$ dominate in the near zone, the terms in $r^{-1}$ in the far zone [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 11.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the near zone the electric field is the static dipole field. It follows the dipole moment without delay. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-near-E}
#### The near zone: a static dipole

For $kr \ll 1$, $e^{ikr} \approx 1$ and the $r^{-3}$ term dominates: $\mathbf E \approx \frac{3\hat{\mathbf n}(\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf p(t)) - \mathbf p(t)}{4\pi r^3}$,
the field of @exm-ems-dipole-limit with the instantaneous moment, as the quasi-static approximation of @exm-emm-quasistatic predicts.
:::

The magnetic field in the near zone is that of the current that changes the dipole. It is weaker than the electric field
by the factor $kr$.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-near-B}
#### The near zone: a current element

For $kr \ll 1$, $\mathbf B \approx \frac{ik}{4\pi r^2}\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf p_0e^{-i\omega t} = \frac{\dot{\mathbf p}\times\hat{\mathbf n}}{4\pi r^2}$, the Biot-Savart field of the
current element $\int\mathbf J = \dot{\mathbf p}$ (@eq-ems-biot-savart); $|\mathbf B|/|\mathbf E| \sim kr \ll 1$.
:::

In the far zone only the $1/r$ terms remain. They are the transverse fields of @prp-emw-dipole-radiation. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-far}
#### The far zone

For $kr \gg 1$, $\mathbf E \approx \frac{k^2}{4\pi r}(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf p_0)\times\hat{\mathbf n}e^{i(kr - \omega t)}$ and $\mathbf B = \hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E$: with
$\ddot{\mathbf p} = -\omega^2\mathbf p$ these are @eq-emw-dipole-field, transverse, in phase and of equal magnitude.
:::

In the induction zone all terms are comparable. The field there is neither static nor a free wave. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-induction}
#### The induction zone

At $kr \sim 1$ the three terms $\frac1{r^3}$, $\frac k{r^2}$, $\frac{k^2}r$ have the same size and different phases; in the equatorial plane the
static and radiation parts of $|\mathbf E|$ are equal at $kr = 1.27$ (@exr-emw-zones-crossover), about a sixth of a wavelength
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 11.3].
:::

The time-averaged energy flux is radial at every distance. The near-zone fields store energy but carry none on average. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-flux}
#### The average flux at every distance

Computing $\langle\mathbf S\rangle = \frac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E\times\bar{\mathbf B})$ from @eq-emw-dipole-full, the cross terms with $\frac1{r^3}$ and $\frac{ik}{r^2}$
are out of phase with $\mathbf B$ and average to zero, leaving $\langle\mathbf S\rangle = \frac{k^4|\mathbf p_0|^2\sin^2\theta}{32\pi^2r^2}\hat{\mathbf n}$ for real $\mathbf
p_0$ at all $r$ (@fig-emw-zones, @exr-emw-zones-flux).
:::

A power line at $50\,$Hz has a wavelength of $6000\,$km. Everything around it is in the near zone. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-power-line}
#### A power line

At $50\,$Hz, $\lambda = 6000\,$km, so the fields of power lines and household wiring are quasi-static everywhere on Earth: their electric and
magnetic fields are those of statics with slowly varying sources, and they radiate a negligible power.
:::

A mobile phone works at gigahertz frequencies. The head of its user is in its near and induction zones. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-phone}
#### A mobile phone

At $1.8\,$GHz, $\lambda = 17\,$cm and $\lambda/2\pi = 2.7\,$cm: a head a few centimetres from the antenna is in the induction zone, where
neither the static nor the radiation approximation holds and the absorbed power must be computed from the full field.
:::

An atom emitting visible light is a tiny source. Its radiation is dipole radiation to excellent accuracy. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-atom}
#### An atom

With $d \approx 0.1\,$nm and $\lambda \approx 500\,$nm, $d/\lambda \approx 2\times10^{-4}$: magnetic dipole and quadrupole transitions are weaker by
$(d/\lambda)^2 \sim 10^{-7}$, which is why atomic selection rules for dipole transitions matter.
:::

In the near zone $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ oscillate a quarter period apart. Energy flows back and forth between the source and the
field.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-reactive}
#### Stored and radiated energy

In the near zone $\mathbf E \propto \mathbf p$ and $\mathbf B \propto \dot{\mathbf p}$ are out of phase, so $\mathbf S$ changes sign twice per period: energy is
stored and returned, the **reactive** field of an antenna, while only the small in-phase part radiates. Far away the fields are in phase
and $\mathbf S$ always points outward.
:::

The far zone also requires the distance to be large compared with the source. The two conditions together define where the
dipole formula holds.

::: {#exm-emw-zones-two-conditions}
#### Two conditions for the far zone

The far-zone formula needs $r \gg \lambda$, for the $1/r$ terms to dominate, and $r \gg d$, for the expansion of @exm-emw-ret-far; for a
large antenna ($d \gtrsim \lambda$) also $r \gg d^2/\lambda$, so that the phase $k\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf x'$ varies negligibly across the
source's projection.
:::
::::

The near-zone magnetic field is the Biot-Savart field of the dipole current. The fourth exercise proves it. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exr-emw-zones-biot-savart}
#### The near zone magnetic field

Show that the Biot-Savart field of a small current distribution with $\int\mathbf J = \dot{\mathbf p}$ is $\frac{\dot{\mathbf p}\times\hat{\mathbf n}}{4\pi r^2}$ at
leading order in $d/r$, and that it is the $kr \ll 1$ limit of $\mathbf B$ in @eq-emw-dipole-full.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In @eq-ems-biot-savart with $|\mathbf x'| \ll r$, $\frac{\mathbf x - \mathbf x'}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|^3} \approx \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}}{r^2}$, giving $\frac{(\int\mathbf
J)\times\hat{\mathbf n}}{4\pi r^2}$. In @eq-emw-dipole-full, $\frac{k^2}r(1 - \frac1{ikr}) \approx \frac{ik}{r^2}$, and $ik\mathbf p_0e^{-i\omega t}\times$ with
$-i\omega\mathbf p_0 = \dot{\mathbf p}$ gives $-\dot{\mathbf p}$, so $\mathbf B \approx -\frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\times\dot{\mathbf p}}{4\pi r^2}$, the same.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

With Sage, expand $E_\theta$ and $B_\varphi$ of a dipole along $\mathbf e_z$ for $kr \ll 1$ and for $kr \gg 1$, and identify the static dipole

\approx -\frac{k^2p_0\sin\theta}{4\pi r}e^{ikr}$ up to the common phase:

The ratio of the magnetic to the electric field distinguishes the zones. The sixth exercise computes it on the equator.

::: {#exr-emw-zones-ratio}
#### $|\mathbf B|/|\mathbf E|$ across the zones

Show that on the equator $\frac{|\mathbf B|}{|\mathbf E|} = \frac{kr\sqrt{1 + (kr)^2}}{\sqrt{1 - (kr)^2 + (kr)^4}}$, which is $\approx kr$ for $kr \ll 1$ and
$\to 1$ for $kr \gg 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the equator $|\mathbf E| = \frac{p_0}{4\pi r^3}|1 - ikr - (kr)^2|$ and $|\mathbf B| = \frac{p_0k}{4\pi r^2}|kr + i|$, with $|1 - ikr - (kr)^2|^2 = (1 -
(kr)^2)^2 + (kr)^2 = 1 - (kr)^2 + (kr)^4$ and $|kr + i|^2 = 1 + (kr)^2$.
:::

#### The full fields of a magnetic dipole

Using the duality $\mathbf E \to \mathbf B$, $\mathbf B \to -\mathbf E$ of the vacuum equations, obtain the full fields of an oscillating magnetic dipole
$\mathbf m_0$ from @eq-emw-dipole-full, and check the static limit.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Replace $\mathbf p_0 \to \mathbf m_0$, $\mathbf E \to \mathbf B$ and $\mathbf B \to -\mathbf E$: $\mathbf B$ has the bracket of $\mathbf E$ in @eq-emw-dipole-full, and $\mathbf E =
-\frac{k^2e^{i(kr - \omega t)}}{4\pi}(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf m_0)\frac1r(1 - \frac1{ikr})$. For $k \to 0$, $\mathbf B$ becomes @eq-ems-magnetic-dipole.

The near-zone energy grows without bound as the distance decreases. The ninth exercise estimates it. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exr-emw-zones-stored}
#### Energy stored near a dipole

Show that the electric energy of the near-zone field outside a sphere of radius $a$ is of order $\frac{p_0^2}{a^3}$ and compare it with the
energy radiated per period, of order $\frac{\omega^3p_0^2}{12}$; deduce that a small antenna ($ka \ll 1$) stores much more energy than it
radiates per cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac12\int_{r > a}|\mathbf E|^2 \sim \frac12\cdot\frac{p_0^2}{16\pi^2}\int_a^\infty\frac{4\pi r^2dr}{r^6} \sim \frac{p_0^2}{24\pi a^3}$, and $\langle P\rangle\frac{2\pi}\omega
= \frac{\omega^3p_0^2}6$; their ratio is of order $(ka)^{-3} \gg 1$: a small antenna has a high quality factor and a narrow bandwidth.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The polarisation of the far field and the near field differ. The last exercise compares them on the equator. Each zone has its own approximation.

::: {#exr-emw-zones-direction}
#### Direction of the field in each zone

For $\mathbf p_0 = p_0\mathbf e_z$, find the direction of $\mathbf E$ on the axis and on the equator in the near and the far zone.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the equator $\mathbf E \parallel -\mathbf e_z$ in both zones. On the axis the far field vanishes ($\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf p_0 = 0$) while the
near field is $\frac{2p_0}{4\pi r^3}(1 - ikr)\mathbf e_z$, longitudinal: there is no radiation along the dipole, only a near field.
:::

### Radiation reaction

A charge that radiates loses energy, so the Lorentz force of the external fields cannot be the whole force on it. The
missing force, the reaction of its own field, is small for every ordinary motion and is found here in outline from the
energy balance; its systematic derivation and its difficulties belong to the theory of the self-force
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 12.3].

The proposition states the Abraham-Lorentz force and the energy balance it reproduces. The characteristic time $\tau$ that
it contains is the time light takes to cross the classical radius of the particle.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emw-radiation-reaction}
#### Abraham-Lorentz force

For a charge $q$ of mass $m$ moving slowly, the force
$$
\mathbf F_{\text{rad}} = \frac{q^2}{6\pi}\dot{\mathbf a} = m\tau\dot{\mathbf a}, \qquad \tau = \frac{q^2}{6\pi m}
$$ {#eq-emw-abraham-lorentz}
($\tau = q^2/6\pi\varepsilon_0mc^3$ in SI units, $6.3\times10^{-24}\,$s for an electron) accounts for the radiated energy:
$\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\mathbf F_{\text{rad}}\cdot\mathbf v\,dt = -\int_{t_1}^{t_2}P\,dt + m\tau[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v]_{t_1}^{t_2}$, with $P$ the Larmor power of
@prp-emw-larmor, so the work of $\mathbf F_{\text{rad}}$ equals minus the radiated energy over a period of a periodic motion, or
between states with equal $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v$. The equation of motion $m\mathbf a = \mathbf F_{\text{ext}} + m\tau\dot{\mathbf a}$ is of third order: besides
the physical solutions it has **runaway** solutions growing as $e^{t/\tau}$, and the physical ones are selected by **reduction of order**,
$\mathbf F_{\text{rad}} \approx \tau\dot{\mathbf F}_{\text{ext}}$, valid when $\mathbf F_{\text{ext}}$ varies slowly on the time scale $\tau$. *Proof.*
$m\tau\dot{\mathbf a}\cdot\mathbf v = m\tau\frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) - m\tau a^2$ and $m\tau a^2 = \frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi} = P$; integrate. Without external
force, $\mathbf a = m\tau\dot{\mathbf a}/m$ gives $\mathbf a = \mathbf a_0e^{t/\tau}$. To first order in $\tau$, $\dot{\mathbf a} = \dot{\mathbf F}_{\text{ext}}/m + O(\tau)$
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 12.3.3-12.3.4; @macchi2023problems, Problem 10.12].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The time $\tau$ is tiny for every known particle. The example gives its value for the electron and the proton.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-tau}
#### The characteristic time

$\tau = \frac{2}{3}\frac{r_e}{c}$ in SI units, with $r_e = 2.82\times10^{-15}\,$m the classical electron radius (@exm-ems-energy-self): $6.3\times10^{-24}\,$s
for the electron and $3.4\times10^{-27}\,$s for the proton. Below such times quantum effects, at the Compton time $\hbar/mc^2 = 1.3\times
10^{-21}\,$s of the electron, set in first, so the classical force is only an approximation.
:::

The energy identity of the proposition is an integration by parts. The boundary term is the Schott energy. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-energy}
#### The energy balance

Over one period of a periodic motion $[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v]$ vanishes and $\int\mathbf F_{\text{rad}}\cdot\mathbf v\,dt = -\int P\,dt$: on average the reaction
force removes exactly the radiated energy. The term $m\tau\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v$, the **Schott energy**, is energy exchanged with the field
near the charge [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 12.3.3].
:::

Without external force the equation still has accelerating solutions. They are the runaway solutions, which no free particle
shows. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-runaway}
#### Runaway solutions

With $\mathbf F_{\text{ext}} = 0$, $\mathbf a = \tau\dot{\mathbf a}$ has $\mathbf a = \mathbf a_0e^{t/\tau}$: unless $\mathbf a_0 = 0$ the particle accelerates exponentially
on its own, gaining kinetic energy while radiating. These solutions are excluded by requiring $\mathbf a \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$ when the
force vanishes.
:::

The physical solution responds to a force slightly before the force acts. The effect is confined to a time $\tau$.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-preacceleration}
#### Preacceleration

Excluding runaways, the solution is $\mathbf a(t) = \frac1{m\tau}\int_t^\infty e^{(t - t')/\tau}\mathbf F_{\text{ext}}(t')\,dt'$. For a force switched on at $t =
0$ the particle starts to accelerate at $t \approx -\tau$: a violation of causality on a scale of $10^{-23}\,$s, where the classical
description fails anyway (@exr-emw-rr-preacceleration).
:::

A charge bound by a spring loses energy by radiation. The reaction force acts as a weak friction. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-oscillator}
#### A radiating oscillator

For $m\ddot x = -m\omega_0^2x + m\tau\dddot x$, reduction of order gives $\dddot x \approx -\omega_0^2\dot x$, so $\ddot x + \omega_0^2\tau\dot x + \omega_0^2x = 0$: a damped
oscillator with energy decay rate $\Gamma = \omega_0^2\tau$ and quality factor $Q = 1/(\omega_0\tau)$, about $5\times10^7$ for visible light
[@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.3].
:::

The damping gives the emitted light a finite width in frequency. Expressed as a wavelength, the classical width is the same
for every line.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-linewidth}
#### The natural linewidth

Light emitted by an oscillator decaying at rate $\Gamma$ has a frequency width $\Delta\omega = \Gamma$, so $\Delta\lambda = \frac{\lambda^2\Delta\omega}{2\pi c} =
2\pi c\tau = 1.2\times10^{-14}\,$m for any $\lambda$; the corresponding lifetime $1/\Gamma$ is about $10\,$ns at $500\,$nm, close to that of
real atomic transitions.
:::

A charge circling in a magnetic field slows down by radiating. Reduction of order turns the reaction force into a drag.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-cyclotron}
#### Damping of cyclotron motion

With $\mathbf F_{\text{ext}} = q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ and circular motion at $\omega = qB/m$, $\dot{\mathbf F}_{\text{ext}} = q\mathbf a\times\mathbf B = -m\omega^2\mathbf v$, so
$\mathbf F_{\text{rad}} \approx -m\tau\omega^2\mathbf v$, a drag whose power $m\tau\omega^2v^2$ is the Larmor power $\frac{q^2\omega^2v^2}{6\pi}$; it gives the
decay of @exm-emw-larmor-cyclotron.
:::

Under a constant force the reaction force vanishes, yet the charge radiates. The energy then comes from the Schott term.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-uniform}
#### Uniform acceleration

For $\mathbf a$ constant, $\dot{\mathbf a} = 0$ and $\mathbf F_{\text{rad}} = 0$, while $P = m\tau a^2 \neq 0$. The balance of the proposition holds through
the Schott term: $\frac{d}{dt}(m\tau\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) = m\tau a^2$, so the radiated energy is drawn from the field near the charge, not from
its kinetic energy (@exr-emw-rr-schott).
:::

The Abraham-Lorentz force is the slow limit of a covariant equation. The relativistic form adds terms that keep the force
orthogonal to the four-velocity.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-ald}
#### The Abraham-Lorentz-Dirac equation

For relativistic motion the reaction force becomes the Abraham-Lorentz-Dirac force, $\frac{q^2}{6\pi}\bigl(\dddot x^\mu + \ddot x^\nu\ddot x_\nu\dot
x^\mu\bigr)$ in terms of proper time, whose spatial part reduces to @eq-emw-abraham-lorentz for $v \ll 1$; it has the same runaway and
preacceleration problems [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 12.3.4-12.3.5].
:::

The reaction force matters only when the external force changes on time scales near $\tau$. The example compares the two forces
for a charge in a wave.

::: {#exm-emw-rr-small}
#### When the reaction is negligible

For a force oscillating at $\omega$, $|\mathbf F_{\text{rad}}| \approx \tau\omega|\mathbf F_{\text{ext}}|$, and $\omega\tau \approx 10^{-8}$ for visible light: the reaction
force is a tiny correction, important only for its cumulative effect on energy, as in the linewidth, or for ultra-intense lasers where
the electron reaches $\gamma \gg 1$.
:::
::::

#### The energy identity

Prove $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}m\tau\dot{\mathbf a}\cdot\mathbf v\,dt = m\tau[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v]_{t_1}^{t_2} - \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi}dt$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) = \dot{\mathbf a}\cdot\mathbf v + a^2$, so $\dot{\mathbf a}\cdot\mathbf v = \frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) - a^2$; multiply by $m\tau$, use
$m\tau = \frac{q^2}{6\pi}$, and integrate.
:::

The classical lifetime of an atomic oscillator is close to measured ones. The fifth exercise evaluates it with Sage. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exr-emw-rr-lifetime}
#### Classical lifetimes and linewidths

With Sage, compute $1/\Gamma$, the quality factor and $\Delta\lambda$ for an electron oscillating at $\lambda = 500\,$nm and at $\lambda = 0.1\,$nm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1/\Gamma = 11\,$ns, $Q = 4.2\times10^7$ at $500\,$nm; $0.45\,$fs and $Q = 8.5\times10^3$ at $0.1\,$nm; $\Delta\lambda = 1.2\times10^{-14}\,$m in both:

{{< sage exr-emw-rr-lifetime >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Reduction of order is a statement about small $\tau$. The sixth exercise justifies it for the oscillator. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exr-emw-rr-reduction}
#### Why reduction of order works

Write $x = x_0 + \tau x_1 + O(\tau^2)$ in $\ddot x + \omega_0^2x = \tau\dddot x$ and show that to first order the equation is that of a damped oscillator
with rate $\omega_0^2\tau$, while the runaway solution is not of this form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At order zero $\ddot x_0 = -\omega_0^2x_0$, so $\dddot x_0 = -\omega_0^2\dot x_0$; at order one $\ddot x_1 + \omega_0^2x_1 = \dddot x_0 = -\omega_0^2\dot x_0$, which is
the same as replacing $\tau\dddot x$ by $-\tau\omega_0^2\dot x$. The runaway $e^{t/\tau}$ is not analytic in $\tau$ at $\tau = 0$ and is missed by
the expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The drag on a circling charge was found by reduction of order. The seventh exercise compares the rate with Larmor's formula.

::: {#exr-emw-rr-cyclotron-check}
#### The cyclotron drag, checked

Show that the drag $-m\tau\omega^2\mathbf v$ of @exm-emw-rr-cyclotron makes the kinetic energy decay as $e^{-2\tau\omega^2t}$, and that this agrees with
@exm-emw-larmor-cyclotron.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{dt}\frac12mv^2 = -m\tau\omega^2v^2 = -2\tau\omega^2\cdot\frac12mv^2$, rate $2\tau\omega^2 = \frac{q^2\omega^2}{3\pi m}$, which is the rate $\frac{e^2\omega^2}{3\pi
m}$ found from Larmor's formula.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A uniformly accelerated charge radiates without a reaction force. The eighth exercise checks the Schott balance. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exr-emw-rr-schott}
#### The Schott energy

For constant $\mathbf a$, show that $\frac{d}{dt}(m\tau\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) = P$ and explain how the energy identity of the proposition holds with
$\mathbf F_{\text{rad}} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) = a^2$ for constant $\mathbf a$, so $\frac{d}{dt}(m\tau\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v) = m\tau a^2 = P$; the identity reads $0 = -\int P\,dt + m\tau[\mathbf
a\cdot\mathbf v]$: the radiated energy equals the increase of the Schott term, taken from the field bound to the charge.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

An electron driven by a wave radiates and feels a reaction force. The ninth exercise finds the phase it causes and the
absorbed power.

::: {#exr-emw-rr-driven}
#### A free electron driven by a wave

For $m\ddot x = qE_0\cos\omega t + m\tau\dddot x$, find the steady solution and show that the power absorbed from the wave equals the scattered power
of @exm-emw-larmor-thomson to first order in $\omega\tau$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 10.12].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x = \operatorname{Re}(\hat xe^{-i\omega t})$, $-m\omega^2\hat x = qE_0 + im\tau\omega^3\hat x$, so $\hat x = -\frac{qE_0}{m\omega^2(1 + i\omega\tau)}$. The velocity amplitude is $\hat v = -i\omega\hat x = \frac{iqE_0}{m\omega(1 + i\omega\tau)}$, and the absorbed power is $\langle qE\dot x\rangle =
\frac12qE_0\operatorname{Re}\hat v = \frac{q^2E_0^2\tau}{2m(1 + \omega^2\tau^2)} \approx \frac{q^2E_0^2\tau}{2m} = \frac{q^4E_0^2}{12\pi m^2}$, the Thomson power.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a relativistic electron in an intense laser the reaction force becomes important. The last exercise estimates when. The reaction force is small but has definite consequences.

::: {#exr-emw-rr-strong}
#### When radiation reaction matters

An electron in a laser field of angular frequency $\omega = 2.4\times10^{15}\,$s$^{-1}$ radiates in each period an energy of order $P\cdot\frac{2\pi}\omega$ with
$P \sim \frac{e^2\gamma^4\omega^2v^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}$ for circular motion. Show that this is comparable to its energy $\gamma mc^2$ when $\gamma^3 \sim
\frac{1}{\omega\tau}$, and evaluate $\gamma$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $v \approx c$, $P\frac{2\pi}\omega \sim 2\pi m\tau\gamma^4\omega c^2$, and the ratio to $\gamma mc^2$ is $2\pi\gamma^3\omega\tau$, of order one for $\gamma \sim
(2\pi\omega\tau)^{-1/3} \approx 220$: reached in today's most intense lasers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The last exercises combine the units of the section. Each follows one physical system from its fields to its radiation and,

::: {#exr-emw-int-hydrogen-line}
#### A classical spectral line

Model an atomic electron as a charge on a spring with $\lambda = 589\,$nm. With Sage, compute the radiated power for an amplitude of $0.1\,$nm, the
decay time, the natural linewidth, and the far-zone field at $1\,$m in the equatorial plane.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle P\rangle = \frac{e^2\omega^4z_0^2}{12\pi\varepsilon_0c^3} \approx 3.0\times10^{-12}\,$W, $1/\Gamma = 15.6\,$ns, $\Delta\lambda = 1.2\times10^{-14}\,$m, and the field amplitude
$\frac{e\omega^2z_0}{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^2r} = 1.6\times10^{-5}\,$V/m:

{{< sage exr-emw-int-hydrogen-line >}}
:::

A synchrotron light source combines Liénard's formula, beaming and the energy balance. The second exercise works out its
numbers. It combines several units of the section.

::: {#exr-emw-int-synchrotron}
#### A synchrotron light source

Electrons of $3\,$GeV circle with radius $\rho = 7\,$m. Find the energy lost per turn with @exm-emw-larmor-synchrotron, the power for a current of
$0.3\,$A, the opening angle of the emission cone, and the characteristic frequency $\gamma^3c/\rho$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma = 5870$, the loss per turn is $\frac{e^2\gamma^4}{3\varepsilon_0\rho} \approx 1.0\,$MeV, so the beam radiates $1.0\,$MeV $\times0.3\,$A $= 0.30\,$MW, in a cone of
$1/\gamma = 0.17\,$mrad, at frequencies around $\gamma^3c/\rho = 8.7\times10^{18}\,$s$^{-1}$, in the X-ray range.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A charge oscillating in a cavity of a radio antenna links the near field, the radiation and the reaction. The last exercise
follows the energy.

::: {#exr-emw-int-antenna}
#### An antenna as a damped oscillator

A short dipole antenna of length $\ell$ is driven at resonance and then left alone. Treating its charge as an oscillator with radiation resistance
$R_{\text{rad}}$ (@exm-emw-dip-antenna) and inductance $L$, find the decay time of the oscillation, and compare the energy stored in the near zone
with that radiated per period (@exr-emw-zones-stored).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The circuit equation $L\dot I + R_{\text{rad}}I + q/C = 0$ gives energy decay at the rate $R_{\text{rad}}/L$, the analogue of $\Gamma$ in
@exm-emw-rr-oscillator. The stored energy exceeds the energy radiated per period by a factor of order $(k\ell)^{-3}$, the quality factor of a
short antenna, so its oscillation lasts many periods.
:::

## Fields in matter {#sec-em-matter}

Inside matter the microscopic fields vary wildly over atomic distances, and what is measured are their averages over
regions containing many atoms. The averaged fields obey Maxwell's equations with the charges and currents of the atoms
included as polarisation and magnetisation; a material is then described by how these respond to the fields, and the
response, which depends on frequency, decides how waves travel, are absorbed, guided and scattered
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Chs. 13-16]. The units are those of @sec-em-statics; in Heaviside-Lorentz units the
vacuum has $\varepsilon = \mu = 1$, and relative permittivities and permeabilities of SI tables are used unchanged.

### Polarisation and magnetisation

An external field displaces the electrons of an atom relative to the nucleus and turns the atom into a small dipole;
it also aligns the magnetic moments of atoms. Averaged over many atoms these dipoles become densities, and their
divergences and curls act as charge and current densities of their own.

![A dielectric sphere with relative permittivity $\varepsilon = 4$ in a uniform field $E_0\mathbf e_z$: field lines of $\mathbf E$ (left)
and of $\mathbf D$ (right) in a plane through the centre, with the magnitude of each field shaded. Inside, $\mathbf E = \frac{3}{\varepsilon + 2}E_0\mathbf e_z$
is uniform and half as strong as far away, while $\mathbf D = \varepsilon\mathbf E$ is twice as strong; the lines of $\mathbf D$ run continuously through
the surface and crowd into the sphere, while most lines of $\mathbf E$ end on the bound surface charge $\sigma_b = P\cos\theta$, and only a few
continue inside. Generated by `figures/emx_dielectric_sphere.sage`.](figures/emx_dielectric_sphere.png){#fig-emx-dielectric-sphere width=95%}

The first definition describes a polarised material by its dipole moment per unit volume. Its bound charges follow from
the potential of a continuum of dipoles.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-emx-polarisation}
#### Polarisation

The **polarisation** $\mathbf P(t, \mathbf x)$ of a material is its electric dipole moment per unit volume. A polarised body $V$ produces
the potential of the **bound charges**
$$
\rho_b = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf P \quad\text{in } V, \qquad \sigma_b = \mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n} \quad\text{on } \partial V ,
$$ {#eq-emx-bound-charge}
and a time-dependent polarisation carries the **polarisation current** $\mathbf J_P = \partial_t\mathbf P$, which satisfies $\partial_t\rho_b +
\nabla\cdot\mathbf J_P = 0$. A material is a **dielectric** when its charges are bound to atoms or molecules, so that its only
response to a static field is a polarisation. In SI units $\mathbf P$ is in C/m$^2$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 13.2;
@pierrus2018solved, Questions 9.2, 10.1-10.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A slab polarised perpendicular to its faces is the simplest polarised body. Its bound charge sits on the two faces.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-slab}
#### A polarised slab

For uniform $\mathbf P = P\mathbf e_z$ in $|z| < d$, $\rho_b = 0$ and $\sigma_b = \pm P$ on $z = \pm d$: two charged planes, so $\mathbf E = -P\mathbf e_z$
inside and $0$ outside (@exm-ems-plane). The field produced by the polarisation opposes it, which is why it is called the
**depolarising field** [@pierrus2018solved, Question 9.4].
:::

A uniformly polarised sphere has a bound surface charge proportional to $\cos\theta$. Its field inside is uniform. This makes the sphere the standard example of a polarised body in the rest of the section.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-sphere}
#### A uniformly polarised sphere

For $\mathbf P = P\mathbf e_z$ in $r < a$, $\sigma_b = P\cos\theta$, which by @exr-ems-uniqueness-sphere-charge (with $3E_0 = P$) gives
$\mathbf E = -\frac{\mathbf P}3$ inside and, outside, the field of the dipole $\mathbf p = \frac{4\pi}3a^3\mathbf P$, the total dipole moment of
the sphere [@macchi2023problems, Problem 3.3].
:::

An atom in a field acquires a dipole proportional to the field. The constant is the atomic polarisability. It links the microscopic picture of a single atom to the macroscopic polarisation of a material.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-atom}
#### Atomic polarisability

An atom in a weak field $\mathbf E$ acquires $\mathbf p = \alpha\mathbf E$. The model of @exm-ems-gauss-overlap, a uniform electron cloud of
radius $a$, gives $\alpha = 4\pi a^3$ ($4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3$ in SI units, @exr-emx-pol-cloud); quantum mechanics gives $\alpha =
4\pi\cdot\frac92a_0^3$ for hydrogen. A gas of $n$ atoms per unit volume then has $\mathbf P = n\alpha\mathbf E$.
:::

Molecules with a permanent dipole are aligned by the field against thermal agitation. The result is a polarisation that
falls with temperature.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-langevin}
#### Polar molecules

A gas of $n$ molecules with permanent dipole $p$ at temperature $T$ in a field $E$ has $P = np\,L(pE/k_BT)$, with the Langevin
function $L(x) = \coth x - \frac1x \approx \frac x3$: for weak fields $P = \frac{np^2}{3k_BT}E$. For water vapour, $p = 6.2\times10^{-30}\,$C m, the
orientational part dominates the atomic one at room temperature [@pierrus2018solved, Question 9.5].
:::

A polarised body is neutral, so its bound charges add up to zero. The example checks it from the definition.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-neutral}
#### Bound charges cancel

$\int_V\rho_b\,d^3x + \oint_{\partial V}\sigma_b\,dS = -\int_V\nabla\cdot\mathbf P + \oint\mathbf P\cdot d\mathbf S = 0$ by the divergence theorem:
polarisation moves charge within the body but creates none. Its dipole moment is $\int_V\mathbf P\,d^3x$, as the definition
requires: the same divergence theorem applied to $x_i\mathbf P$ gives $\int_V x_i\rho_b\,d^3x + \oint x_i\sigma_b\,dS = \int_V P_i\,d^3x$.
:::

A non-uniform polarisation leaves a bound charge in the volume. The example computes it for a polarisation that grows
linearly.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-nonuniform}
#### A non-uniform polarisation

For $\mathbf P = kx\mathbf e_x$ in the cube $0 < x, y, z < L$, $\rho_b = -k$ throughout the volume and $\sigma_b = kL$ on the face $x = L$ and
$0$ on the others: the face carries $kL^3$, which cancels the volume charge $-kL^3$.
:::

When the polarisation changes in time, the moving bound charges form a current. It is the source that radiates in
@prp-emw-dipole-radiation.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-current}
#### The polarisation current

$\partial_t\rho_b + \nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P = -\partial_t\nabla\cdot\mathbf P + \nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P = 0$: the bound charges are conserved with the
current $\partial_t\mathbf P$. For a small body, $\int\partial_t\mathbf P\,d^3x = \dot{\mathbf p}$, the current whose time derivative is the source of dipole
radiation [@pierrus2018solved, Questions 10.1-10.2].
:::

A lattice of small conducting spheres behaves as a dielectric. Each sphere is a dipole induced by the field. Such artificial dielectrics are used to build lenses for microwaves, whose wavelengths are much longer than the spheres.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-artificial}
#### An artificial dielectric

Conducting spheres of radius $a$, $n$ per unit volume and far apart, acquire $\mathbf p = 4\pi a^3\mathbf E$ each (@exm-ems-conductor-sphere-field),
so $\mathbf P = 4\pi na^3\mathbf E$ and $\chi_e = 4\pi na^3$, three times the volume fraction they occupy; microwave lenses use such
materials [@macchi2023problems, Problem 3.1].
:::

A long cylinder polarised across its axis has a uniform field inside, like the sphere. The depolarising factor is $\frac12$
instead of $\frac13$.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-cylinder}
#### A transversely polarised cylinder

For $\mathbf P = P\mathbf e_x$ in an infinite cylinder of radius $a$, $\sigma_b = P\cos\varphi$, and the two-dimensional analogue of
@exm-emx-pol-sphere gives $\mathbf E = -\frac{\mathbf P}2$ inside: the depolarising factors of a slab, a cylinder and a sphere are $1$, $\frac12$ and
$\frac13$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 3.11].
:::

The polarisation is a macroscopic average. The microscopic field inside a dielectric is very different from the averaged
field used here.

::: {#exm-emx-pol-averaging}
#### Macroscopic averages

The macroscopic fields are averages of the microscopic ones over regions large compared with atoms ($\sim1\,$nm) and small
compared with the scale of variation of the fields; they satisfy Maxwell's equations with averaged sources, which are the
free charges and the bound charges of @eq-emx-bound-charge [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 13.1-13.2].
:::
