The impulse response of the Lorentz oscillator is a damped oscillation. The third exercise derives it with Sage. The impulse response vanishes before the impulse, as causality requires.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-impulse}
#### The impulse response

With Sage, solve $\ddot x + \gamma\dot x + \omega_0^2x = \frac{e}{m}E_0\delta(t)$ for $x = 0$ before the pulse, deduce $\chi(t)$ for $n$ electrons per unit
volume, and check that its transform is $\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The pulse gives $\dot x(0^+) = eE_0/m$, so $x = \frac{eE_0}{m\tilde\omega}e^{-\gamma t/2}\sin\tilde\omega t$, and $\chi = \frac{ne^2}{m\tilde\omega}e^{-\gamma t/2}\sin
\tilde\omega t$; its transform is the stated function:

{{< sage exr-emx-kk-impulse >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The absorbed power is given by the imaginary part. The fourth exercise derives it. The answer is the cycle average of the work done by the field on the charges.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-absorption}
#### Absorbed power

For $\mathbf E = \operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E_0e^{-i\omega t})$ and $\mathbf P = \operatorname{Re}(\hat\chi\mathbf E_0e^{-i\omega t})$, show that $\langle\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P\rangle =
\frac\omega2\operatorname{Im}\hat\chi|\mathbf E_0|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_t\mathbf P = \operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\hat\chi\mathbf E_0e^{-i\omega t})$, and @exm-emw-pw-averages gives $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{\mathbf E_0}\cdot(-i\omega\hat\chi)\mathbf
E_0) = \frac\omega2\operatorname{Im}\hat\chi|\mathbf E_0|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The f-sum rule can be checked on a single oscillator. The fifth exercise does it with Sage. The integral of the absorption weighted by the frequency is fixed by the plasma frequency alone.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-sum-rule}
#### The sum rule for one oscillator

With Sage, compute $\int_0^\infty\omega\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)\,d\omega$ for $\varepsilon = 1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}$ and compare
with $\frac\pi2\omega_p^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The integral is $\frac\pi2\omega_p^2$ for any $\omega_0$ and $\gamma$:

{{< sage exr-emx-kk-sum-rule >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The static sum rule relates the static permittivity to absorption. The sixth exercise checks it for the oscillator. It follows from the first relation evaluated at zero frequency.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-static}
#### The static sum rule

Show that $\frac2\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)}\omega d\omega = \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2}$ for the Lorentz oscillator, which is $\varepsilon(0) - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon}\omega = \frac{\omega_p^2\gamma}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}$, and the integral over $(0, \infty)$ is $\frac{\pi\omega_p^2}{2\omega_0^2}$
by residues (@thm-residue), giving $\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2} = \varepsilon(0) - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The reality condition follows directly from the definition. The seventh exercise asks for it and for its consequence on the
refractive index.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-symmetry}
#### Symmetry of the permittivity

Prove $\varepsilon(-\omega) = \overline{\varepsilon(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, and deduce that the refractive index $n(\omega) = \sqrt{\varepsilon(\omega)}$ has an even real part
and an odd imaginary part.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The reality of $\chi$ gives the first. With the branch of the square root continuous from $\omega = 0$, $n(-\omega) = \overline{n(\omega)}$, which is the
second statement.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Hilbert transform pairs of the relations can be checked on simple functions. The eighth exercise uses a pole. The transform of a simple pole below the real axis is known in closed form.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-pole}
#### A single pole

Show that $f(\omega) = \frac{1}{\omega_1 - \omega - i\Gamma}$, $\Gamma > 0$, is holomorphic in the upper half plane, and verify that its real and imaginary parts are
related by $f(\omega) = \frac1{\pi i}\mathrm P\int\frac{f(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega}d\omega'$ at $\omega = \omega_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The pole is at $\omega = \omega_1 - i\Gamma$, in the lower half plane. At $\omega = \omega_1$, $f = \frac{i}\Gamma$, and $\mathrm P\int\frac{d\omega'}{(\omega_1 - \omega' - i\Gamma)(\omega' -
\omega_1)} = \mathrm P\int\frac{-du}{u(u + i\Gamma)} = -\frac\pi\Gamma$ (with $u = \omega' - \omega_1$, the odd part dropping out), so $\frac1{\pi i}(-\frac\pi\Gamma) = \frac
i\Gamma$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Microwave heating rests on the Debye absorption of water. The ninth exercise estimates the absorbed power. The oven frequency lies well below the peak of the water absorption.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-microwave}
#### Microwave heating

With $\Delta\varepsilon = 75$ and $\tau_0 = 8\,$ps, compute $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon$ at $2.45\,$GHz and the power absorbed per unit volume in a field of amplitude
$10^3\,$V/m, in SI units ($\frac12\omega\varepsilon_0\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon E_0^2$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega\tau_0 = 0.12$, $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon = \frac{75\cdot0.12}{1.015} = 9.1$, and the absorbed power is $\frac12\cdot1.54\times10^{10}\cdot8.85\times10^{-12}\cdot9.1\cdot10^6
\approx 6\times10^5\,$W/m$^3$: a glass of water absorbs tens of watts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The relations fail for an acausal response. The last exercise checks it on the example. The real part computed from the relations differs from the true one.

::: {#exr-emx-kk-acausal}
#### The relations need causality

For $\hat\chi = \frac{2\tau_0}{1 + \omega^2\tau_0^2}$ (@exm-emx-kk-acausal), compute the right-hand side of the second relation and show that it is not zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\operatorname{Re}\hat\chi$ even and positive, $-\frac{2\omega}\pi\mathrm P\int_0^\infty\frac{\operatorname{Re}\hat\chi(\omega')}{\omega'^2 - \omega^2}d\omega' = \frac{2\omega\tau_0^2}{1 +
\omega^2\tau_0^2} \neq 0$ by residues, while $\operatorname{Im}\hat\chi = 0$: the relation fails.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The simplest microscopic model of the response treats every electron as a damped harmonic oscillator driven by the
field. It reproduces dielectrics and, with zero restoring force, metals.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-emx-drude-lorentz}
#### Drude-Lorentz model

In the **Drude-Lorentz model** the electrons of a medium, $n$ per unit volume, are oscillators with resonance frequencies $\omega_j$,
damping rates $\gamma_j$ and fractions $f_j$ ($\sum_jf_j = 1$), obeying $m\ddot{\mathbf x} = -e\mathbf E - m\omega_j^2\mathbf x - m\gamma_j\dot{\mathbf x}$; then
$$
\varepsilon(\omega) = 1 + \omega_p^2\sum_j\frac{f_j}{\omega_j^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma_j\omega}, \qquad \omega_p^2 = \frac{ne^2}m ,
$$ {#eq-emx-drude-lorentz}
with the **plasma frequency** $\omega_p$ ($\omega_p^2 = ne^2/\varepsilon_0m$ in SI units). The **Drude model** of a metal is the case of free electrons,
$\omega_j = 0$, $\gamma_j = \gamma$, equivalent to the conductivity $\sigma(\omega) = \frac{ne^2}{m(\gamma - i\omega)}$ and $\varepsilon(\omega) = 1 -
\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega + i\gamma)}$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 14.3-14.5; @pierrus2018solved, Question 10.8].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A single resonance gives the typical shape of a dielectric. Below it the index rises with frequency, across it the
material absorbs.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-single}
#### One resonance

For one oscillator, $\operatorname{Re}\varepsilon = 1 + \frac{\omega_p^2(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}$ rises with $\omega$ below $\omega_0$
(**normal dispersion**), falls across the resonance (**anomalous dispersion**), and $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon$ is a peak of width $\gamma$ at $\omega_0$
(@fig-emx-dispersion).
:::

Glass is transparent in the visible because its resonances are in the ultraviolet. Expanding the model gives Cauchy's
empirical formula.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-cauchy}
#### Cauchy's formula

For $\omega \ll \omega_0$ and negligible damping, $n^2 = \varepsilon \approx 1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2}\bigl(1 + \frac{\omega^2}{\omega_0^2}\bigr)$: the index grows slowly
with frequency, so blue light is refracted more than red, which is why a prism separates colours (@exr-emx-dl-cauchy).
:::

Copper is described well by the Drude model up to the visible. Its parameters follow from the electron density and the
static conductivity.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-copper}
#### Drude parameters of copper

With $n = 8.5\times10^{28}\,$m$^{-3}$, $\omega_p = \sqrt{ne^2/\varepsilon_0m} = 1.6\times10^{16}\,$s$^{-1}$ ($\hbar\omega_p = 11\,$eV), and $\sigma_0 = 6\times10^7\,$S/m
gives $\gamma = \frac{ne^2}{m\sigma_0} = 4\times10^{13}\,$s$^{-1}$, a collision time of $25\,$fs [@pierrus2018solved, Question 10.8].
:::

The ionosphere is a dilute plasma. Its plasma frequency separates the radio waves it reflects from those it lets through.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-ionosphere}
#### The ionosphere

With $n \approx 10^{12}\,$m$^{-3}$ electrons, $f_p = \frac{\omega_p}{2\pi} \approx 9\,$MHz: short waves below this frequency are reflected and travel around the
Earth, while FM and satellite signals pass through [@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.14].
:::

The Drude model gives the static conductivity and its frequency dependence. At low frequency the metal is a resistor. At high frequency the inertia of the electrons dominates.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-conductivity}
#### The Drude conductivity

From $m\dot{\mathbf v} = -e\mathbf E - m\gamma\mathbf v$ with $\mathbf J = -ne\mathbf v$, $\sigma(\omega) = \frac{ne^2}{m(\gamma - i\omega)}$: real and constant, $\sigma_0 =
\frac{ne^2}{m\gamma}$, for $\omega \ll \gamma$, and imaginary (inductive) for $\omega \gg \gamma$, where the electrons respond by their inertia
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 14.4].
:::

Above its plasma frequency a metal becomes transparent. The alkali metals let ultraviolet light through. The threshold is set by the density of the conduction electrons.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-transparency}
#### Ultraviolet transparency of metals

For $\omega \gg \gamma$, $\varepsilon \approx 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}$, negative below $\omega_p$ and positive above. Sodium, with one free electron per atom ($n =
2.65\times10^{28}\,$m$^{-3}$), has $\lambda_p = 2\pi c/\omega_p = 205\,$nm, and indeed becomes transparent below about $210\,$nm
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 14.5].
:::

At very high frequency all electrons behave as free. The permittivity tends to one from below. This is why the refractive index of matter for X-rays is slightly below one.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-xrays}
#### X-rays

For $\omega$ far above every resonance, $\varepsilon \approx 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}$ with all $Z$ electrons per atom in $n$: the index is slightly below one,
$1 - n \sim 10^{-6}$ for X-rays in glass, which allows total external reflection of X-rays at grazing incidence.
:::

The fractions $f_j$ add up to one. This is the classical version of the oscillator-strength sum rule. It expresses that each electron contributes once to the total response.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-strengths}
#### Oscillator strengths

With $\sum_jf_j = 1$, @eq-emx-drude-lorentz satisfies the f-sum rule of @exm-emx-kk-sum-rule for every choice of resonances: the total absorption depends only on
$n$. In quantum mechanics the $f_j$ become transition strengths, still summing to the number of electrons.
:::

A dilute gas has $\varepsilon$ close to one. Its refractive index differs from one by half the susceptibility. The resulting index is close to the measured values for air and other gases.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-gas}
#### The index of a gas

For $|\chi| \ll 1$, $n = \sqrt{1 + \chi} \approx 1 + \frac\chi2$: air at visible frequencies has $n - 1 = 2.9\times10^{-4}$, from oxygen and nitrogen
resonances in the far ultraviolet; the index varies with pressure through $n$.
:::

The Drude-Lorentz model includes the static polarisability. At zero frequency each oscillator gives the polarisability of
@exm-emx-pol-atom. The static limit therefore agrees with the polarisability found earlier.

::: {#exm-emx-dl-static}
#### The static limit

At $\omega = 0$, @eq-emx-drude-lorentz gives $\varepsilon(0) = 1 + \frac{ne^2}m\sum\frac{f_j}{\omega_j^2}$, the polarisability $\alpha = \frac{e^2}{m\omega_0^2}$ per electron
with one resonance; the cloud model of @exr-emx-pol-cloud has $\omega_0^2 = \frac{e^2}{4\pi ma^3}$, the same.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises start with the Lorentz oscillator. The first one derives @eq-emx-drude-lorentz. The derivation solves the equation of motion of a bound electron in an oscillating field.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-derive}
#### Deriving the permittivity

Solve $m\ddot{\mathbf x} = -e\mathbf E_0e^{-i\omega t} - m\omega_0^2\mathbf x - m\gamma\dot{\mathbf x}$ in the steady state, and deduce $\mathbf P = -ne\mathbf x$ and
$\varepsilon(\omega)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbf x = \frac{-e\mathbf E_0/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}e^{-i\omega t}$, so $\mathbf P = \frac{ne^2/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\mathbf E$ and $\varepsilon = 1 +
\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Copper's Drude parameters can be computed from tables. The second exercise does it with Sage. The density of conduction electrons and the conductivity are the only inputs.

With Sage, compute $\omega_p$, $\hbar\omega_p$ in eV, $\gamma$ from $\sigma_0 = 5.96\times10^7\,$S/m, and $\operatorname{Re}\varepsilon$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon$ at $\lambda = 600\,$nm
in the Drude model, for $n = 8.5\times10^{28}\,$m$^{-3}$.

$\omega_p = 1.64\times10^{16}\,$s$^{-1}$, $10.8\,$eV, $\gamma = 4.0\times10^{13}\,$s$^{-1}$, and at $600\,$nm $\varepsilon \approx -26 + 0.35i$; the real copper has interband absorption that the model misses, which gives it its colour:

With Sage, compute $f_p$ for electron densities $10^{10}$, $10^{12}$ and $10^{29}\,$m$^{-3}$, and the corresponding wavelengths [@macchi2023problems,

$f_p = 0.90\,$MHz, $9.0\,$MHz and $2.8\times10^{15}\,$Hz; $\lambda_p = 330\,$m, $33\,$m and $106\,$nm:

Cauchy's formula follows by expansion. The fourth exercise derives its coefficients. The expansion is valid well below the resonance frequency of the glass.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-cauchy}
#### Cauchy's coefficients

For one undamped resonance, expand $n(\lambda) = \sqrt{\varepsilon}$ for $\omega \ll \omega_0$ as $A + \frac B{\lambda^2}$, and find $A$ and $B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n^2 \approx 1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2} + \frac{\omega_p^2\omega^2}{\omega_0^4}$; with $n_0^2 = 1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2}$, $n \approx n_0 + \frac{\omega_p^2\omega^2}{2n_0\omega_0^4}$, so $A =
n_0$ and $B = \frac{2\pi^2\omega_p^2}{n_0\omega_0^4}$ with $\omega = 2\pi/\lambda$ ($2\pi c/\lambda$ in SI units).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Drude conductivity changes character at $\omega = \gamma$. The fifth exercise checks the two regimes with Sage. The two regimes are those of a resistor and of a free electron gas.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-conductivity}
#### Low and high frequency

With Sage, expand $\sigma(\omega) = \frac{\sigma_0}{1 - i\omega/\gamma}$ for $\omega \ll \gamma$ and $\omega \gg \gamma$, and show that $\varepsilon = 1 + \frac{i\sigma}\omega$ equals the
Drude form of @eq-emx-drude-lorentz.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma \approx \sigma_0(1 + i\omega/\gamma)$ and $\sigma \approx \frac{i\sigma_0\gamma}\omega$; and $1 + \frac{i\sigma}\omega = 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega + i\gamma)}$ with $\sigma_0 =
\frac{\omega_p^2}\gamma$:

{{< sage exr-emx-dl-conductivity >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Sodium becomes transparent in the ultraviolet. The sixth exercise computes the threshold. It uses one conduction electron per atom and the density of the metal.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-sodium}
#### The transparency threshold of sodium

Sodium has density $970\,$kg/m$^3$ and atomic mass $23$. Assuming one free electron per atom, find $n$, $\omega_p$ and $\lambda_p$ in SI units.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n = \frac{970}{23\times1.66\times10^{-27}} = 2.5\times10^{28}\,$m$^{-3}$, $\omega_p = 9.0\times10^{15}\,$s$^{-1}$ and $\lambda_p = 210\,$nm, close to the observed
threshold.

The width of the absorption peak is the damping rate. The seventh exercise checks it. The width is measured at half the maximum height of the peak.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-width}
#### Width of the absorption line

Show that for $\gamma \ll \omega_0$, $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon$ falls to half its maximum at $\omega \approx \omega_0 \pm \frac\gamma2$, and find the height of the peak.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Near $\omega_0$, $(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 \approx 4\omega_0^2(\omega - \omega_0)^2$, so $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon \approx \frac{\omega_p^2\gamma\omega_0}{4\omega_0^2(\omega - \omega_0)^2 + \gamma^2\omega_0^2}$, a
Lorentzian of full width $\gamma$ and height $\frac{\omega_p^2}{\gamma\omega_0}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The energy of the electrons in a plasma wave is part of the wave's energy. The eighth exercise compares it with the field
energy.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-electron-energy}
#### Energy of a free electron gas in a wave

For a transverse wave in a collisionless plasma, show that the time-averaged kinetic energy of the electrons per unit volume is $\frac{\omega_p^2}{4\omega^2}|\mathbf
E_0|^2$, and that adding it to $\frac14(|\mathbf E_0|^2 + |\mathbf B_0|^2)$ gives the dispersive energy density of @exm-emx-en-dispersive
[@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.2].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbf v = \frac{-e\mathbf E_0}{-im\omega}e^{-i\omega t}$, so $\langle\frac12nmv^2\rangle = \frac{ne^2}{4m\omega^2}|\mathbf E_0|^2 = \frac{\omega_p^2}{4\omega^2}|\mathbf E_0|^2$. With $\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega} =
1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}$ for $\varepsilon = 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}$, $\frac14\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega}|\mathbf E_0|^2 = \frac14|\mathbf E_0|^2 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{4\omega^2}|\mathbf E_0|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Two resonances combine additively. The ninth exercise finds the transparent window between them. Between the resonances the medium is transparent and normally dispersive.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-two-resonances}
#### A window between two resonances

For $\varepsilon = 1 + \frac{1}{1 - \omega^2} + \frac{1}{9 - \omega^2}$ (no damping), find where $\varepsilon < 0$ (no propagation) and where it is positive between the
resonances.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x = \omega^2$, $\varepsilon = 0$ gives $(1 - x)(9 - x) + (9 - x) + (1 - x) = x^2 - 12x + 19 = 0$, so $x = 6 \mp \sqrt{17}$, $\omega = 1.37$ and
$3.18$. Just above each resonance the corresponding term is large and negative: $\varepsilon < 0$ for $1 < \omega < 1.37$ and $3 < \omega < 3.18$, and the
medium is transparent for $\omega < 1$, between $1.37$ and $3$, and above $3.18$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Drude model fails for semiconductors without a correction for the lattice. The last exercise includes a background
permittivity. The background accounts for the polarisation of the bound electrons.

::: {#exr-emx-dl-background}
#### A background permittivity

In a doped semiconductor $\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_\infty - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}$ (no damping) with $\varepsilon_\infty = 12$. Find the frequency below which it reflects,
and its value for $n = 10^{24}\,$m$^{-3}$ electrons of effective mass $0.07m_e$, in SI units.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\varepsilon = 0$ at $\omega = \omega_p/\sqrt{\varepsilon_\infty}$. With $\omega_p = \sqrt{ne^2/\varepsilon_0m^*} = 2.1\times10^{14}\,$s$^{-1}$, the edge is at $6.1\times10^{13}\,$s$^{-1}$,
a wavelength of $31\,\mu$m, in the infrared.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Waves in matter

In a homogeneous medium the plane waves of @def-emw-plane-wave survive with a wave number set by the response of the
medium at the wave's frequency. A complex permittivity makes the wave decay, and a negative one stops it; metal walls
guide waves along a tube.

![Left, the reflectivity $R = |(n - 1)/(n + 1)|^2$ at normal incidence of a Drude metal with $\gamma = 0.01\,\omega_p$ against $\omega/\omega_p$: nearly total
below the plasma frequency, where $n$ is almost imaginary, and falling to almost zero above it. Right, the dispersion relation $\omega^2 = \omega_p^2 +
k^2$ of transverse waves in a collisionless plasma (and, with $\omega_p$ replaced by the cut-off $\pi/a$, of the $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ mode of a waveguide), with
the light line $\omega = k$: the phase velocity $\omega/k$ exceeds $1$, the group velocity $d\omega/dk$ is below it. Generated by
`figures/emx_waves.sage`.](figures/emx_waves.svg){#fig-emx-waves width=95%}

The proposition gives the plane waves of a linear medium and the two velocities that describe them. The permittivity can
include conduction, as in @exm-emx-kk-conductor.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emx-waves-media}
#### Waves in a linear medium

In a homogeneous linear medium without free charges, with $\varepsilon(\omega)$ and $\mu(\omega)$ (conduction included in $\varepsilon$), the fields
$\mathbf E = \operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E_0e^{i(kz - \omega t)})$, $\mathbf B = \operatorname{Re}(\frac k\omega\mathbf e_z\times\mathbf E_0e^{i(kz - \omega t)})$ with $\mathbf E_0\perp\mathbf
e_z$ solve @eq-emx-macroscopic if and only if
$$
k^2 = \varepsilon(\omega)\mu(\omega)\omega^2, \qquad k = n(\omega)\omega, \qquad n = n_r + i\kappa = \sqrt{\varepsilon\mu} ,
$$ {#eq-emx-dispersion}
($k = n\omega/c$ in SI units). The intensity decays as $e^{-2\kappa\omega z}$; the **phase velocity** is $v_p = \omega/\operatorname{Re}k = 1/n_r$ and the
**group velocity**, the speed of a wave packet of nearby frequencies in a transparent medium, is $v_g = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \bigl(\frac{d(n_r\omega)}{d\omega}\bigr)^{-1}$.
In a good conductor ($\sigma \gg \omega$) $k \approx \frac{1 + i}\delta$ with the **skin depth** $\delta = \sqrt{2/\mu\sigma\omega}$; in a collisionless plasma ($\varepsilon = 1 -
\omega_p^2/\omega^2$) waves propagate only for $\omega > \omega_p$. *Proof.* Insert into Faraday's law, $\omega\mathbf B_0 = k\mathbf e_z\times\mathbf E_0$, and into the
Ampère-Maxwell law with $\mathbf D = \varepsilon\mathbf E$, $\mathbf H = \mathbf B/\mu$: $k\mathbf e_z\times\mathbf B_0/\mu = -\omega\varepsilon\mathbf E_0$, which with the first gives
$k^2 = \varepsilon\mu\omega^2$. A packet $\int a(k)e^{i(kz - \omega(k)t)}dk$ peaked at $k_0$ moves with $d\omega/dk$ by stationary phase. For $\varepsilon \approx
i\sigma/\omega$, $k^2 = i\mu\sigma\omega$ and $\sqrt i = \frac{1 + i}{\sqrt2}$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 15.1-15.3; @pierrus2018solved, Questions
10.10-10.11].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In glass light is slower than in vacuum. The phase velocity is the inverse of the refractive index. The wavelength inside the glass is shorter by the same factor.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-glass}
#### Light in glass

For glass with $n = 1.5$ and $\mu = 1$, light travels at $c/1.5 = 2\times10^8\,$m/s and its wavelength shrinks by $1.5$; the frequency is unchanged, being fixed
by the source. $|\mathbf B| = n|\mathbf E|$ in Heaviside-Lorentz units, so the magnetic part of the energy equals the electric part (@exr-emx-en-equipartition).
:::

Metals screen alternating fields within the skin depth. At power frequencies it is millimetres, at microwave frequencies
micrometres. This is why thin metal sheets can screen microwaves completely.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-skin}
#### The skin depth of copper

In SI units $\delta = \sqrt{2/\mu_0\sigma\omega}$: for copper $9.2\,$mm at $50\,$Hz, $66\,\mu$m at $1\,$MHz and $2.1\,\mu$m at $1\,$GHz, which is why high-frequency
currents flow in a thin surface layer and cables are silver-plated [@pierrus2018solved, Question 10.11].
:::

The fraction of light reflected at a boundary depends on the indices on the two sides. At normal incidence the formula is
simple.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-reflection}
#### Reflection at normal incidence

Matching tangential $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ at the surface of a medium with index $n$ ($\mu = 1$) gives the reflected amplitude $r = \frac{1 - n}{1 + n}$
(@exr-emx-wv-fresnel): $R = |r|^2 = 4\%$ for glass, $2\%$ for water, and $R \to 1$ for a metal with $|n| \gg 1$.
:::

A metal is a mirror for light below its plasma frequency. The permittivity is negative there and the wave cannot enter.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-metal-mirror}
#### Why metals shine

For $\gamma \ll \omega < \omega_p$, $\varepsilon \approx 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2} < 0$, so $n \approx i\sqrt{\omega_p^2/\omega^2 - 1}$ is imaginary and $R = |\frac{1 - n}{1 + n}|^2 = 1$:
total reflection, with the field decaying within $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega_p^2 - \omega^2}}$, about $20\,$nm for silver (@fig-emx-waves)
[@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 15.3.1].
:::

In a plasma the phase velocity exceeds that of light. The group velocity, which carries the signal, does not. The product of the two velocities is one in natural units.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-plasma}
#### Phase and group velocity in a plasma

From $\omega^2 = \omega_p^2 + k^2$, $v_p = \frac\omega k = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \omega_p^2/\omega^2}} > 1$ and $v_g = \frac{k}\omega = \sqrt{1 - \omega_p^2/\omega^2} < 1$, with $v_pv_g =
1$: radio pulses through the interstellar plasma arrive later at lower frequency, which measures the electron column density to pulsars
(@fig-emx-waves) [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 15.2].
:::

In a dispersive transparent medium the group velocity is set by the group index. For glass it exceeds the ordinary index.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-group-index}
#### The group index of glass

$v_g = 1/n_g$ with $n_g = n + \omega\frac{dn}{d\omega} = n - \lambda\frac{dn}{d\lambda}$; with Cauchy's formula $n = A + B/\lambda^2$ (@exm-emx-dl-cauchy), $n_g = A +
3B/\lambda^2$. For a glass with $A = 1.50$, $B = 4.2\times10^{-15}\,$m$^2$ at $500\,$nm, $n = 1.517$ and $n_g = 1.550$.
:::

Near an absorption line the group velocity can exceed one, or become negative. Signals still do not travel faster than
light.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-anomalous}
#### Anomalous dispersion

Across a resonance $dn_r/d\omega < 0$, so $v_g$ can exceed $1$; the packet is then strongly absorbed and reshaped, and the front of a signal, governed by $\varepsilon
\to 1$ at high frequency, travels at exactly $1$, as causality (@prp-emx-kramers-kronig) requires [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 15.2].
:::

Sea water absorbs radio waves within metres. Submarines communicate at very low frequencies. Their low frequency gives them a skin depth of several metres.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-sea-water}
#### Radio waves in sea water

With $\sigma = 4\,$S/m, sea water is a good conductor below about $1\,$GHz, and $\delta = \sqrt{2/\mu_0\sigma\omega}$ is $0.25\,$m at $1\,$MHz but $25\,$m at $100\,$Hz:
only extremely low frequencies reach submerged submarines (@exr-emx-wv-sea).
:::

At the plasma frequency a plasma supports oscillations without any wave vector constraint. They are longitudinal waves. They are the plasma oscillations of the electron gas as a whole.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-longitudinal}
#### Longitudinal waves

A longitudinal field $\mathbf E \parallel \mathbf k$ has $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D = i\varepsilon\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E = 0$, possible only if $\varepsilon(\omega) = 0$: in a plasma at $\omega = \omega_p$, the
plasma oscillation of @exr-ems-plasma-oscillation, with no magnetic field [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 15.3.2; @macchi2023problems, Problem 11.3].
:::

A layer of a quarter wavelength cancels the reflection from a lens. The two reflected waves interfere destructively. The coating has a refractive index between those of air and glass.

::: {#exm-emx-wv-coating}
#### An anti-reflection coating

A film of index $n_1 = \sqrt{n_2}$ and thickness $\lambda/4n_1$ on glass of index $n_2$ reflects at its two faces with equal amplitudes and a phase difference of $\pi$:
the reflection vanishes at that wavelength. For $n_2 = 1.5$, $n_1 = 1.22$, close to magnesium fluoride's $1.38$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.5].
:::

The reflection coefficient follows from the boundary conditions. The third exercise derives it. The derivation uses the continuity of the tangential fields at normal incidence.

::: {#exr-emx-wv-fresnel}
#### Reflection at normal incidence

A wave $E_0e^{i(z - \omega t)}$ in vacuum meets a medium of index $n$ ($\mu = 1$) at $z = 0$. Write reflected and transmitted waves, impose the continuity of $E_x$ and
$H_y$, and find $r$ and $t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$E_0 + E_r = E_t$ and, with $H = nE$ in the medium and $H = \pm E$ for the waves in vacuum, $E_0 - E_r = nE_t$. So $r = \frac{1 - n}{1 + n}$ and $t = \frac{2}{1 + n}$,
with $|r|^2 + n|t|^2 = 1$ for real $n$ (energy conservation).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The group velocity in a plasma decreases toward the plasma frequency. The fourth exercise computes the delay of a radio pulse
with Sage.

::: {#exr-emx-wv-dispersion-delay}
#### Dispersion of pulsar signals

A pulse travels a distance $L$ through a plasma with $\omega_p \ll \omega$. Show with Sage that the arrival time is $L(1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{2\omega^2})$ to first order, and
evaluate the extra delay between $400\,$MHz and $800\,$MHz for $nL = 10^{24}\,$m$^{-2}$ (SI units, $t = L/v_g c$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1/v_g = (1 - \omega_p^2/\omega^2)^{-1/2} \approx 1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{2\omega^2}$, so the delay is $\frac{L\omega_p^2}{2c\omega^2} = \frac{e^2nL}{2\varepsilon_0mc\omega^2}$: $0.84\,$s at $400\,$MHz and
$0.21\,$s at $800\,$MHz, a difference of $0.63\,$s:

{{< sage exr-emx-wv-dispersion-delay >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The group index of glass follows from Cauchy's formula. The fifth exercise derives it. The group index exceeds the refractive index in normal dispersion.

::: {#exr-emx-wv-group-index}
#### The group index

Show that $n_g = n - \lambda\frac{dn}{d\lambda}$, and that for $n = A + B/\lambda^2$, $n_g = A + 3B/\lambda^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$k = n\omega$ and $\frac{dk}{d\omega} = n + \omega\frac{dn}{d\omega}$; with $\omega \propto 1/\lambda$, $\omega\frac{d}{d\omega} = -\lambda\frac{d}{d\lambda}$. Then $-\lambda\frac{dn}{d\lambda} =
\frac{2B}{\lambda^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

$R = 0.98$ at $0.5$ and $0.87$ at $0.99$, then a sharp drop to $0.56$ at $1.01$, $0.17$ at $1.1$ and $0.005$ at $2$ (@fig-emx-waves):

A good conductor has $\mathbf B$ larger than $\mathbf E$ and out of phase. The eighth exercise finds the ratio.

::: {#exr-emx-wv-conductor-fields}
#### Fields in a good conductor

For $k = \frac{1 + i}\delta$, find $|\mathbf B|/|\mathbf E|$ and the phase between them, and show that the magnetic energy dominates [@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.13].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbf B_0 = \frac k\omega\mathbf e_z\times\mathbf E_0$, so $\frac{|B|}{|E|} = \frac{\sqrt2}{\omega\delta} = \sqrt{\sigma/\omega} \gg 1$ (with $\mu = 1$) and $\mathbf B$ lags $\mathbf E$ by $45^\circ$;
the magnetic energy exceeds the electric one by $\sigma/\omega$.
:::

The anti-reflection condition follows from the amplitudes at the two interfaces. The ninth exercise derives it. The reflected amplitudes from the two surfaces must be equal and opposite.

::: {#exr-emx-wv-coating}
#### The quarter-wave coating

Using $r_{ab} = \frac{n_a - n_b}{n_a + n_b}$ and neglecting multiple reflections, show that a film of index $n_1$ and optical thickness $\lambda/4$ on a substrate $n_2$
cancels the reflection when $n_1 = \sqrt{n_2}$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.5].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two reflections $r_{01} = \frac{1 - n_1}{1 + n_1}$ and $r_{12} = \frac{n_1 - n_2}{n_1 + n_2}$ differ in path by half a wavelength, a sign; they cancel when
$\frac{n_1 - 1}{n_1 + 1} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{n_2 + n_1}$, which gives $n_1^2 = n_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A metal film thinner than the skin depth lets some light through. The last exercise estimates it. The transmitted intensity falls exponentially with the ratio of the thickness to the skin depth.

::: {#exr-emx-wv-foil}
#### A thin metal foil

A silver film with field decay length $20\,$nm in the visible is $50\,$nm thick. Estimate the fraction of the intensity that crosses it, ignoring multiple
reflections but including the reflection at the first surface ($R \approx 0.95$) [@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.4].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The transmitted intensity is about $(1 - R)e^{-2\cdot50/20} = 0.05\cdot e^{-5} \approx 3\times10^{-4}$, enough to see a bright lamp through a gold-leaf or silver
film.
:::

::::

A hollow metal tube carries waves only above a frequency fixed by its size. The proposition finds the modes of a guide of any
cross-section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emx-waveguide}
#### Waveguide modes

In a hollow, perfectly conducting tube along $\mathbf e_z$ with cross-section $\Sigma$, fields $\propto e^{i(k_zz - \omega t)}$ in vacuum split into **TE modes** ($E_z
= 0$) with $B_z = \psi(x, y)$, $(\nabla_\perp^2 + \gamma^2)\psi = 0$ and $\partial_n\psi = 0$ on $\partial\Sigma$, and **TM modes** ($B_z = 0$) with $E_z = \psi$ and $\psi = 0$ on
$\partial\Sigma$; in both, $\omega^2 = k_z^2 + \gamma^2$, so a mode propagates only above its **cut-off** $\omega_c = \gamma$, with group velocity $k_z/\omega < 1$ and phase
velocity $\omega/k_z > 1$. A hollow guide has no TEM mode. For a rectangle $0 < x < a$, $0 < y < b$, $\gamma_{mn} = \pi\sqrt{m^2/a^2 + n^2/b^2}$, with $m, n \geq 0$ not both
zero for TE and $m, n \geq 1$ for TM; the lowest mode is $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ with $\omega_c = \pi/a$ ($\pi c/a$ in SI units). *Proof.* The transverse fields follow from
$E_z$, $B_z$ by the curl equations, the boundary conditions $\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E = 0$, $\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf B = 0$ on the walls become the stated conditions on $\psi$,
and the wave equation gives $\nabla_\perp^2\psi = (k_z^2 - \omega^2)\psi$. A TEM mode would have $\mathbf E_\perp = -\nabla_\perp\phi$ with $\phi$ harmonic in $\Sigma$ and constant
on the single boundary, hence zero [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 15.4; @pierrus2018solved, Questions 7.12-7.13].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The lowest mode of a rectangular guide has a simple field. Its electric field is a half sine across the wide side.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-te10}
#### The $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ mode

For $\psi = B_0\cos(\pi x/a)$, $E_y = E_0\sin(\pi x/a)\cos(k_zz - \omega t)$ with $E_0 = \frac{\omega a}\pi B_0$, $B_x = -\frac{k_z}\omega E_y$ and $B_z = B_0\cos(\pi x/a)\sin(k_zz - \omega t)$:
$E_y$ vanishes on the walls $x = 0, a$ and is tangent nowhere else, as required (@exr-emx-wg-check) [@pierrus2018solved, Question 7.13].
:::

A standard X-band guide carries microwaves between about $8$ and $12\,$GHz. Its cut-offs follow from its dimensions. Below the lower limit no mode propagates in the guide.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-x-band}
#### An X-band waveguide

For $a = 22.86\,$mm and $b = 10.16\,$mm, $f_c(\mathrm{TE}_{10}) = c/2a = 6.56\,$GHz, $f_c(\mathrm{TE}_{20}) = 13.1\,$GHz and $f_c(\mathrm{TE}_{01}) = 14.8\,$GHz: between
$6.6$ and $13.1\,$GHz only one mode propagates, which avoids mixing modes of different speeds.
:::

The waveguide mode is a superposition of plane waves bouncing between the walls. Their angle depends on the frequency. At the cut-off they bounce back and forth without advancing.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-bouncing}
#### Modes as bouncing waves

$\sin(\pi x/a)e^{i(k_zz - \omega t)} = \frac1{2i}(e^{i(\pi x/a + k_zz)} - e^{i(-\pi x/a + k_zz)})e^{-i\omega t}$: two plane waves with $|\mathbf k| = \omega$ at angles $\pm\theta$ from the
axis, $\cos\theta = k_z/\omega$. The group velocity $\cos\theta$ is the axial component of their speed, and at cut-off they bounce perpendicular to the axis
[@macchi2023problems, Problem 12.5].
:::

Near cut-off the energy travels slowly. The group velocity vanishes at the cut-off frequency. The phase velocity at the same time grows without bound.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-velocities}
#### Velocities in a guide

From $\omega^2 = k_z^2 + \omega_c^2$, $v_g = \sqrt{1 - \omega_c^2/\omega^2}$ and $v_p = 1/v_g$: at twice the cut-off frequency $v_g = 0.87$, and below cut-off $k_z$ is
imaginary and the field decays along the guide as $e^{-\sqrt{\omega_c^2 - \omega^2}z}$, an evanescent wave.
:::

A coaxial cable has two conductors and carries a TEM wave at every frequency. It is the guide without a cut-off.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-coax}
#### The TEM mode of a coaxial cable

Between coaxial conductors, $\phi = V\frac{\ln(b/s)}{\ln(b/a)}$ (@exm-ems-uniqueness-coax) times $e^{i(kz - \omega t)}$ with $k = \sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}\omega$ gives a TEM wave, possible
because the cross-section has two boundaries. Its impedance $\frac VI = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac\mu\varepsilon}\ln\frac ba$, $60\,\Omega\,\frac{\ln(b/a)}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}$ in SI
units, is $50\,\Omega$ for polyethylene with $b/a = 3.5$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 12.1].
:::

A square guide has degenerate modes. Two polarisations share the lowest cut-off. The degeneracy is lifted when one side is made longer.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-square}
#### A square guide

For $a = b$, $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ and $\mathrm{TE}_{01}$ have the same cut-off $\pi/a$ and fields at right angles: any combination propagates, including circularly
polarised ones, which is useful for rotating joints but makes the guide sensitive to small deformations [@macchi2023problems, Problem 12.4].
:::

The lowest TM mode needs both indices to be at least one. Its cut-off is higher than that of the lowest TE mode.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-tm11}
#### The lowest TM mode

$E_z = E_0\sin\frac{\pi x}a\sin\frac{\pi y}b$ vanishes on all walls, with $\gamma_{11} = \pi\sqrt{a^{-2} + b^{-2}}$, above $\gamma_{10}$: TM modes appear only at higher
frequencies in a rectangular guide.
:::

Closing a guide at both ends makes a resonant cavity. Its modes have discrete frequencies. Microwave ovens and the accelerating structures of particle accelerators are cavities of this kind.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-cavity}
#### A rectangular cavity

With conducting walls also at $z = 0$ and $z = d$, $k_z = p\pi/d$ and $\omega_{mnp} = \pi\sqrt{(m/a)^2 + (n/b)^2 + (p/d)^2}$: a microwave oven, about $30\,$cm wide, has
many modes near $2.45\,$GHz, and a rotating plate averages over their hot spots.
:::

The space between the Earth and the ionosphere is a spherical cavity. Its lowest resonances are at a few hertz.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-schumann}
#### Schumann resonances

For a thin spherical shell of radius $R$ the lowest modes have $\omega_l \approx \frac{\sqrt{l(l + 1)}}R$ ($c/R$ in SI units), so $f_1 = \frac{\sqrt2c}{2\pi R} = 10.6\,$Hz;
lightning excites them, and the observed $7.8\,$Hz is lower because the ionosphere is a lossy conductor [@macchi2023problems, Problem 12.8].
:::

Filling a guide with a dielectric lowers its cut-off. The waves inside are slower. The cut-off frequency is divided by the refractive index of the filling.

::: {#exm-emx-wg-filled}
#### A filled waveguide

With a medium $\varepsilon$, $\mu$ inside, $\varepsilon\mu\omega^2 = k_z^2 + \gamma^2$ and the cut-off becomes $\gamma/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$: a guide filled with polyethylene ($\varepsilon =
2.25$) passes frequencies $1.5$ times lower [@macchi2023problems, Problem 12.7].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises start with the $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ fields. The first one checks them with Sage. The fields must satisfy the wave equation and the boundary conditions on the walls.

#### The $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ mode, checked

With Sage, take $E_y = E_0\sin(\pi x/a)\cos(kz - \omega t)$, compute $\mathbf B$ from Faraday's law, and check the vacuum equations and the boundary conditions on the
walls.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbf B = (-\frac k\omega E_y, 0, \frac{\pi E_0}{\omega a}\cos\frac{\pi x}a\sin(kz - \omega t))$; the equations hold for $\omega^2 = k^2 + \pi^2/a^2$, $E_y = 0$ and $B_x = 0$ on $x = 0,
a$:

{{< sage exr-emx-wg-check >}}

Below cut-off the field decays along the guide. The fourth exercise estimates the decay for a waveguide window. The decay length is comparable to the width of the guide.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-evanescent}
#### An evanescent wave

A $2.45\,$GHz microwave oven has holes of $2\,$mm in its door. Treating each hole as a guide with cut-off $c/2a$ for $a = 2\,$mm, find the decay length of the field and
the attenuation through a $1\,$mm thick door.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f_c = 75\,$GHz $\gg 2.45\,$GHz, so $|k_z| \approx \pi/a = 1.6\times10^3\,$m$^{-1}$, a decay length of $0.64\,$mm, and the amplitude drops by $e^{-1.6} = 0.2$ per mm; many holes and
a thicker mesh give the observed shielding.
:::

The bouncing-wave picture gives the group velocity geometrically. The fifth exercise asks for the angle. The angle follows from the ratio of the cut-off to the frequency.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-angle}
#### The angle of the bouncing waves

For the $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ mode at frequency $\omega$, find the angle of the two plane waves of @exm-emx-wg-bouncing with the axis, and show that the time a wavefront takes to
advance a length $L$ along the guide is $L/v_g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sin\theta = \frac{\pi/a}\omega = \frac{\omega_c}\omega$. Each plane wave moves at speed $1$ along its direction, which has axial component $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \omega_c^2/\omega^2}
= v_g$, so the energy advances $L$ in time $L/\cos\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The impedance of a coaxial cable follows from its capacitance and inductance. The sixth exercise checks the TEM speed. The speed equals that of light in the dielectric of the cable.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-coax}
#### Speed and impedance of a cable

Using the capacitance and the inductance per unit length of a coaxial cable filled with $\varepsilon$, $\mu$ (@exr-ems-int-coax), show that the TEM speed is
$1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ and the impedance $\sqrt{L/C}$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}\ln\frac ba$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$C = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}$, $L = \frac{\mu}{2\pi}\ln\frac ba$; the telegraph equation gives speed $1/\sqrt{LC} = 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ and impedance $\sqrt{L/C} =
\frac{\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$, which in SI units is $60\,\Omega\sqrt{\mu_r/\varepsilon_r}\ln\frac ba$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The modes of a cavity are standing waves. The seventh exercise counts them with Sage. The count grows as the cube of the frequency at high frequency.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-cavity}
#### Modes of a cubic cavity

With Sage, count the modes $(m, n, p)$ of a cubic cavity of side $30\,$cm with frequencies between $2.40$ and $2.50\,$GHz, counting two polarisations when all three
indices are non-zero and one otherwise.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are twelve modes in this band, from the permutations of $(2, 2, 4)$ and $(0, 3, 4)$, so the field pattern in a microwave oven is a superposition of several standing waves:

{{< sage exr-emx-wg-cavity >}}

A hollow guide cannot carry a TEM wave, while a cable can. The eighth exercise proves the first statement. The proof uses the fact that a field without sources inside a closed conductor vanishes.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-no-tem}
#### No TEM wave in a hollow guide

Show that a TEM mode ($E_z = B_z = 0$) has $\nabla_\perp\times\mathbf E_\perp = 0$ and $\nabla_\perp\cdot\mathbf E_\perp = 0$, so $\mathbf E_\perp = -\nabla_\perp\phi$ with $\phi$ harmonic, and
conclude that it vanishes in a guide whose cross-section has a single boundary.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $z$ component of Faraday's law gives $\nabla_\perp\times\mathbf E_\perp = -\partial_tB_z = 0$ and Gauss's law gives $\nabla_\perp\cdot\mathbf E_\perp = -\partial_zE_z = 0$. On the single
conducting boundary $\phi$ is constant, and a harmonic function constant on the whole boundary is constant (@prp-ems-uniqueness), so $\mathbf E_\perp = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

An optical fibre guides light by total internal reflection. The ninth exercise finds the acceptance angle. The angle depends on the refractive indices of the core and the cladding.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-fibre}
#### An optical fibre

A fibre has core index $n_1 = 1.48$ and cladding $n_2 = 1.46$. Find the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary and the largest angle from the axis of light entering
from air that is guided [@macchi2023problems, Problem 12.6].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Total reflection needs $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$, $\theta_c = 80.6^\circ$ from the normal, so the ray makes at most $9.4^\circ$ with the axis inside; Snell's law at the entrance gives
$\sin\alpha = n_1\sin9.4^\circ = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} = 0.24$, $\alpha = 14^\circ$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A cavity loses energy through the walls. The last exercise estimates its quality factor from the skin depth. The quality factor is the ratio of the volume to the skin depth times the area, up to a factor of order one.

::: {#exr-emx-wg-q}
#### The quality factor of a cavity

For a cavity of size $L$ with copper walls, the energy is stored in a volume $\sim L^3$ and dissipated in a layer of thickness $\delta$ on an area $\sim L^2$. Estimate $Q \sim
L/\delta$ for $L = 3\,$cm at $10\,$GHz.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta = 0.66\,\mu$m at $10\,$GHz, so $Q \sim 3\times10^{-2}/6.6\times10^{-7} \approx 5\times10^4$, the order of measured values for copper cavities.
:::

### Scattering of radiation

A wave falling on an electron or a molecule makes it oscillate, and the oscillation radiates in all directions. The ratio of
the scattered power to the incident intensity is an area, the cross-section, which the model of @def-emx-drude-lorentz
computes for every frequency.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-emx-scattering}
#### Scattering by a bound electron

The **scattering cross-section** of a body is $\sigma = P_s/I$, the scattered power divided by the incident intensity, and $\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \frac{dP_s/d\Omega}{I}$. An
electron bound with frequency $\omega_0$ and damping $\gamma$ (@def-emx-drude-lorentz), in a wave of frequency $\omega$ polarised along $\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}$, has
$$
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = r_e^2\frac{\omega^4}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}\sin^2\Theta, \qquad \sigma = \sigma_T\frac{\omega^4}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 +
\gamma^2\omega^2} ,
$$ {#eq-emx-scattering}
with $\Theta$ the angle between $\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}$ and the direction of observation, $r_e = \frac{e^2}{4\pi m}$ and $\sigma_T = \frac{8\pi}3r_e^2$ (@exm-emw-larmor-thomson).
For unpolarised light $\sin^2\Theta$ is replaced by $\frac{1 + \cos^2\theta}2$, $\theta$ the scattering angle. The limits are **Thomson scattering**, $\sigma = \sigma_T$ for $\omega
\gg \omega_0$, and **Rayleigh scattering**, $\sigma = \sigma_T(\omega/\omega_0)^4$ for $\omega \ll \omega_0$. *Proof.* The steady state of @exr-emx-dl-derive gives the dipole
$\mathbf p = \frac{e^2/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\mathbf E_0e^{-i\omega t}$, whose radiation (@prp-emw-dipole-radiation) has $\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = \frac{\omega^4|\mathbf
p_0|^2}{32\pi^2}\sin^2\Theta$ on average; divide by $I = \frac12E_0^2$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Secs. 16.1-16.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Free electrons scatter all frequencies equally. Their cross-section is the Thomson value. It is independent of the frequency as long as the electron moves slowly.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-thomson}
#### Thomson scattering

For $\omega \gg \omega_0$ (or free electrons, $\omega_0 = 0$, with $\gamma \ll \omega$), $\sigma = \sigma_T = 6.65\times10^{-29}\,$m$^2$, independent of frequency: it limits the
transparency of the Sun's interior (@exr-emw-larmor-thomson) and of the early universe before recombination [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 16.2].
:::

Molecules scatter visible light weakly because their resonances lie in the ultraviolet. The fourth power of the frequency
colours the sky.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-rayleigh}
#### Rayleigh scattering

For $\omega \ll \omega_0$, $\sigma = \sigma_T(\omega/\omega_0)^4$: with $\omega_0$ in the ultraviolet, blue light is scattered several times more than red
(@exm-emw-dip-rayleigh). For an N$_2$ molecule at $500\,$nm the measured $\sigma \approx 5\times10^{-31}\,$m$^2$ corresponds to an attenuation length of about $80\,$km in air
at sea level (@exr-emx-sc-sky).
:::

At resonance the cross-section becomes huge. With purely radiative damping it is of the order of the square of the wavelength.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-resonance}
#### Resonance scattering

At $\omega = \omega_0$, $\sigma = \sigma_T\frac{\omega_0^2}{\gamma^2}$. If the damping is the radiative one, $\gamma = \omega_0^2\tau$ (@exm-emw-rr-oscillator), then $\sigma = \frac{8\pi r_e^2}{3\omega_0^2\tau^2} =
\frac{6\pi}{\omega_0^2} = \frac{3\lambda^2}{2\pi}$, independent of the charge: an atom at resonance scatters light from an area $10^{8}$ times its own size.
:::

The scattered light is polarised. At right angles to the incident beam the polarisation is complete. This polarisation of the sky can be seen with polarising sunglasses.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-polarisation}
#### Polarisation of scattered light

For unpolarised incident light, the factor $\frac{1 + \cos^2\theta}2$ is the average of $1$ (polarisation perpendicular to the scattering plane) and $\cos^2\theta$ (in the plane):
at $\theta = 90^\circ$ only the perpendicular part survives, and skylight at $90^\circ$ from the Sun is polarised (@exr-emw-larmor-scattered-polarisation).
:::

A small dielectric sphere scatters like a molecule. Its polarisability is that of the sphere in a uniform field. Its cross-section grows as the sixth power of the radius.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-sphere}
#### A small dielectric sphere

A sphere of radius $a \ll \lambda$ and permittivity $\varepsilon$ acquires $\mathbf p = 4\pi a^3\frac{\varepsilon - 1}{\varepsilon + 2}\mathbf E$ (@exm-emx-mm-sphere), so $\sigma = \frac{8\pi}3k^4a^6\bigl(\frac{\varepsilon -
1}{\varepsilon + 2}\bigr)^2$: dust and droplets much smaller than the wavelength scatter as $\lambda^{-4}$, larger ones less selectively, which is why clouds are white.
:::

A conducting sphere also has a magnetic dipole induced by the wave. Both dipoles contribute to its cross-section. The magnetic dipole points opposite to the magnetic field of the wave.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-conducting-sphere}
#### A small conducting sphere

For a perfectly conducting sphere, $\mathbf p = 4\pi a^3\mathbf E$ and, from the exclusion of the magnetic field, $\mathbf m = -2\pi a^3\mathbf B$; the two radiate together, with total
$\sigma = \frac{10\pi}3k^4a^6$ and a backward-peaked pattern [@macchi2023problems, Problems 10.14-10.15].
:::

Many scatterers remove light from a beam. The intensity decays exponentially with the number of scatterers crossed. The rate of decay is the density of scatterers times their cross-section.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-extinction}
#### Extinction

A beam crossing $n$ scatterers per unit volume loses $nI\sigma\,dx$ per unit area in a length $dx$, so $I = I_0e^{-n\sigma x}$ (Beer's law), with the **mean free path** $1/n\sigma$:
the sunset is red because the path through the atmosphere is long and the blue is scattered out.
:::

At low frequency the bound electron behaves as a static polarisability. The Rayleigh law is the radiation of that induced dipole.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-static-limit}
#### Rayleigh scattering and the static polarisability

For $\omega \ll \omega_0$, $\mathbf p \approx \alpha\mathbf E$ with $\alpha = \frac{e^2}{m\omega_0^2}$ (@exm-emx-dl-static), and $\sigma = \frac{\omega^4\alpha^2}{6\pi}$: the
cross-section depends only on the static polarisability, which is how the scattering by any small neutral body is computed.
:::

When the photon energy is comparable to the electron's rest energy the classical result fails. The example states the
correction qualitatively.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-compton}
#### The limit of classical scattering

Thomson's formula assumes that the electron's recoil is negligible, $\hbar\omega \ll mc^2 = 511\,$keV. For X- and $\gamma$-rays the scattered light changes
frequency (Compton effect) and the cross-section decreases, effects of quantum electrodynamics.
:::

Scattering by many molecules adds incoherently in a gas but coherently in a dense medium. Coherent forward scattering produces
the refractive index.

::: {#exm-emx-sc-coherent}
#### Scattering and refraction

In a dense, uniform medium the waves scattered sideways by neighbouring molecules cancel, and only the forward-scattered waves survive; they add to the incident wave
with a phase lag, which is the slowing of light by the index $n$ of @exm-emx-dl-gas. Density fluctuations restore sideways scattering, as in the blue sky.
:::
::::

The resonance cross-section with radiative damping is universal. The fourth exercise derives it. At resonance the cross-section depends only on the wavelength.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-resonance}
#### The universal resonance cross-section

Show that with $\gamma = \omega_0^2\tau$ and $\tau = \frac{e^2}{6\pi m}$, $\sigma(\omega_0) = \frac{6\pi}{\omega_0^2}$, and evaluate it in SI units for the sodium line at $589\,$nm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma_T\frac{\omega_0^2}{\gamma^2} = \frac{e^4}{6\pi m^2}\cdot\frac{36\pi^2m^2}{e^4\omega_0^2} = \frac{6\pi}{\omega_0^2}$, i.e. $\frac{3\lambda^2}{2\pi} = 1.7\times10^{-13}\,$m$^2$ with $\lambda = 589\,$nm.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The Rayleigh law follows from the static polarisability. The fifth exercise checks the equivalence. The polarisability is expressed through the refractive index of the gas.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-rayleigh-alpha}
#### Rayleigh from the polarisability

Show that $\sigma_T(\omega/\omega_0)^4 = \frac{\omega^4\alpha^2}{6\pi}$ for $\alpha = \frac{e^2}{m\omega_0^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{\omega^4}{6\pi}\frac{e^4}{m^2\omega_0^4} = \frac{e^4}{6\pi m^2}\frac{\omega^4}{\omega_0^4} = \sigma_T\frac{\omega^4}{\omega_0^4}$.
:::

The scattering by small particles depends strongly on their size. The sixth exercise compares a droplet with a molecule. The droplet contains many molecules that scatter coherently.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-droplet}
#### A water droplet and a molecule

With @exm-emx-sc-sphere, compare the cross-section of a water droplet ($\varepsilon = 1.78$ at optical frequencies) of radius $20\,$nm with that of an N$_2$ molecule at $500\,$nm, in SI
units.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$k = 1.26\times10^7\,$m$^{-1}$, $k^4a^6 = 1.6\times10^{-18}$, $(\frac{\varepsilon - 1}{\varepsilon + 2})^2 = 0.043$, so $\sigma = \frac{8\pi}3\cdot1.6\times10^{-18}\cdot0.043 \approx 5.7\times
10^{-19}\,$m$^2$, $10^{12}$ times a molecule's: a few droplets dominate the scattering of humid air.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The polarisation of the scattered light depends on the angle. The seventh exercise computes the degree of polarisation with Sage.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-degree}
#### Degree of polarisation of scattered light

With Sage, compute the degree of polarisation $\frac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{1 + \cos^2\theta}$ of light scattered at angle $\theta$ from unpolarised light, and evaluate it at $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$
and $90^\circ$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$0.14$, $0.60$ and $1$:

{{< sage exr-emx-sc-degree >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Beer's law follows from the definition of the cross-section. The eighth exercise derives it. The derivation considers a thin slab of scatterers crossed by the beam.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-beer}
#### Beer's law

Derive $I = I_0e^{-n\sigma x}$ for a beam crossing a dilute medium of independent scatterers, and state when it fails.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In a slab $dx$ of unit area there are $n\,dx$ scatterers, each removing $\sigma I$, so $dI = -n\sigma I\,dx$. It fails when scattering is coherent (dense media,
@exm-emx-sc-coherent) or when scattered light is scattered back into the beam (multiple scattering).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Thomson cross-section limits the luminosity of stars. The ninth exercise derives the Eddington limit. At that luminosity the radiation pressure balances gravity.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-eddington}
#### The Eddington luminosity

Radiation of luminosity $L$ pushes the electrons of ionised hydrogen with the force $\frac{L\sigma_T}{4\pi r^2c}$ per electron, while gravity pulls the protons with $\frac{GMm_p}{r^2}$. Find
the largest luminosity of a star of mass $M$ and evaluate it for one solar mass, in SI units.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Balance gives $L_E = \frac{4\pi cGMm_p}{\sigma_T} = 1.3\times10^{31}\,$W for $M = 2\times10^{30}\,$kg, $3\times10^4$ solar luminosities.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Coherent forward scattering produces the index of refraction. The last exercise estimates $n - 1$ for a gas from the scattered
amplitude.

::: {#exr-emx-sc-index}
#### The index from forward scattering

For a dilute gas with polarisability $\alpha$ per molecule, show that the forward-scattered waves of a slab of thickness $dz$ add a phase $\frac{n\alpha\omega}{2}dz$ to the
incident wave, which is the index $1 + \frac{n\alpha}2$ of @exm-emx-dl-gas.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A plane wave crossing a sheet of dipoles $\mathbf p = \alpha\mathbf E$ with surface density $n\,dz$ receives the field of the sheet, which by @exr-emw-ret-oscillating-sheet with the
polarisation current $-i\omega n\alpha E\,dz$ is $\frac{i\omega n\alpha}{2}E\,dz$; this is a phase change $\frac{\omega n\alpha}{2}dz = \omega(n_{\text{index}} - 1)dz$, so $n_{\text{index}} - 1 = \frac{n\alpha}2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-electromagnetism-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this section combine the four parts of the chapter. Each follows one physical situation from the static
fields through Maxwell's equations and radiation to the response of matter.

A charge that moves through a medium faster than light does there radiates even at constant velocity. The first exercise
combines the fields of moving charges with the index of refraction.

::: {#exr-emc-cherenkov}
#### Cherenkov radiation

In a medium of index $n$, a charge moving with constant speed $v > 1/n$ outruns its own field. Using the retarded-time construction of @prp-emw-lienard-wiechert
with light speed $1/n$, show that the wavefronts emitted along the path form a cone with $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{nv}$. With Sage, find the threshold kinetic energy of an electron in
water ($n = 1.33$) and the maximal angle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Light emitted at time $t'$ has travelled $\frac{t - t'}n$ while the charge travelled $v(t - t')$; the envelope of the spheres is a cone with $\cos\theta = \frac{1/n}{v}$. The threshold is $v = 1/n$,
$\gamma = (1 - n^{-2})^{-1/2} = 1.52$, a kinetic energy of $0.26\,$MeV, and the maximal angle, for $v \to 1$, is $\arccos\frac1n = 41^\circ$:

{{< sage exr-emc-cherenkov >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A superconductor expels magnetic fields from its interior. The second exercise derives the penetration depth from the canonical momentum of
@def-emm-minimal-coupling and Ampère's law.

::: {#exr-emc-london}
#### The London penetration depth

In a superconductor the electrons condense into a state with zero canonical momentum, $m\mathbf v - e\mathbf A = 0$ for charge $-e$ in the Coulomb gauge. Show that $\mathbf J = -\frac{ne^2}m\mathbf A$,
that static fields obey $\nabla^2\mathbf B = \mathbf B/\lambda_L^2$ with $\lambda_L = \sqrt{m/ne^2} = 1/\omega_p$, and evaluate $\lambda_L$ with Sage for $n = 10^{28}\,$m$^{-3}$ (SI: $\lambda_L = c/\omega_p$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\mathbf v = -e\mathbf A/m$ (sign of the charge included), $\mathbf J = -ne\mathbf v = -\frac{ne^2}m\mathbf A$. Taking the curl of $\nabla\times\mathbf B = \mathbf J$: $-\nabla^2\mathbf B = -\frac{ne^2}m\mathbf B$, so
fields decay as $e^{-x/\lambda_L}$ into the material. For $n = 10^{28}\,$m$^{-3}$, $\lambda_L = 53\,$nm:

{{< sage exr-emc-london >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

An intense laser cannot enter a plasma denser than a critical value. The third exercise combines the Drude model with the dispersion relation.

::: {#exr-emc-critical-density}
#### The critical density

With Sage, find the electron density at which $\omega_p$ equals the frequency of light of wavelength $1\,\mu$m and $0.35\,\mu$m, and compare with the electron density of solid aluminium,
$1.8\times10^{29}\,$m$^{-3}$. What happens to the laser at the surface of the solid?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n_c = \frac{\varepsilon_0m\omega^2}{e^2} = 1.1\times10^{27}$ and $9.1\times10^{27}\,$m$^{-3}$, far below the solid: the laser is reflected at the layer where the expanding plasma reaches $n_c$
(@exm-emx-wv-metal-mirror), and absorbed only near it:

{{< sage exr-emc-critical-density >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At high frequency the current in a wire flows near its surface. The fourth exercise combines the skin depth with the energy flow into the wire.

::: {#exr-emc-skin-resistance}
#### The resistance of a wire at high frequency

A copper wire of radius $a = 1\,$mm carries an alternating current at $1\,$MHz. With the skin depth of @exm-emx-wv-skin, estimate the ratio of its resistance to the direct-current
value, and explain with @exm-emm-poynting-wire where the dissipated energy enters [@macchi2023problems, Problem 6.14].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The current flows in a layer of thickness $\delta = 66\,\mu$m around the circumference, so $R_{\text{ac}}/R_{\text{dc}} \approx \frac{\pi a^2}{2\pi a\delta} = \frac a{2\delta} = 7.6$. The energy enters from
outside through the Poynting vector at the surface and is absorbed within $\delta$, where $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf J$ are confined.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A capacitor filled with water absorbs microwaves. The fifth exercise combines the Debye permittivity, the capacitor and the absorbed power.

::: {#exr-emc-lossy-capacitor}
#### A capacitor filled with water

A parallel-plate capacitor of empty capacitance $C_0 = 1\,$pF is filled with water described by the Debye model of @exm-emx-kk-debye. With Sage, find the complex admittance
$-i\omega\varepsilon(\omega)C_0$ at $50\,$Hz and $2.45\,$GHz, and the power absorbed at $10\,$V amplitude in each case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle P\rangle = \frac12\omega C_0\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon\,V^2$: about $3\times10^{-15}\,$W at $50\,$Hz, where water is a nearly lossless dielectric with $\varepsilon \approx 76$, and $7\,$W at
$2.45\,$GHz, where $\varepsilon = 74.9 + 9.1i$:

{{< sage exr-emc-lossy-capacitor >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Earth's magnetic field stores energy outside the planet. The sixth exercise uses the dipole field and the magnetostatic energy.

::: {#exr-emc-earth-energy}
#### The energy of the Earth's field

With the dipole moment of @exm-ems-dipole-earth and the formula $\frac{\mu_0m^2}{12\pi R^3}$ for the energy of a dipole field outside a sphere of radius $R$
(@exr-ems-int-rotating-sphere in SI units), estimate the magnetic energy outside the Earth, and compare it with a day of the Sun's power received by the Earth, $1.5\times10^{22}\,$J.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{\mu_0m^2}{12\pi R^3} = \frac{1.26\times10^{-6}\cdot6.4\times10^{45}}{12\pi\cdot2.6\times10^{20}} \approx 8\times10^{17}\,$J, twenty thousand times less than a day of sunlight.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A magnetised plasma rotates the polarisation of a wave. The seventh exercise combines circular polarisation with the Drude model in a magnetic field.

::: {#exr-emc-faraday-rotation}
#### Faraday rotation

In a plasma in a magnetic field $B$ along the direction of propagation, the electrons move under $m\dot{\mathbf v} = -e(\mathbf E + \mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$. Show that the two circular
polarisations of @exm-emw-pol-circular see $\varepsilon_\pm = 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega \mp \omega_c)}$, $\omega_c = eB/m$, and that a linear polarisation rotates by
$\frac{\omega_p^2\omega_c}{2\omega^2}$ per unit length for $\omega \gg \omega_p, \omega_c$ [@macchi2023problems, Problem 11.7].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $\mathbf E = E(\mathbf e_x \pm i\mathbf e_y)$, the velocity is circular and the magnetic force shifts the effective frequency, giving $\mathbf v = \frac{-ie\mathbf E}{m(\omega \mp \omega_c)}$ (the sign
depending on the sense of rotation relative to the electron's cyclotron motion), hence $\varepsilon_\pm$. The wave numbers $k_\pm = \omega\sqrt{\varepsilon_\pm} \approx \omega - \frac{\omega_p^2}{2\omega}(1 \pm \frac{\omega_c}\omega)$
differ by $\frac{\omega_p^2\omega_c}{\omega^2}$, and a linear wave, the sum of the two, rotates by half the phase difference per unit length.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A transmission line carries a wave between two conductors. The eighth exercise combines the static capacitance and inductance with the wave equation and
reflection.

::: {#exr-emc-transmission-line}
#### A transmission line

A line has inductance $L$ and capacitance $C$ per unit length. From $\partial_zV = -L\partial_tI$ and $\partial_zI = -C\partial_tV$, derive waves of speed $1/\sqrt{LC}$ and impedance $Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}$,
and show that a load $Z_L$ at the end reflects the amplitude $\frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0}$ [@macchi2023problems, Problems 7.6, 12.1].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating, $\partial_z^2V = LC\partial_t^2V$. A wave $V = f(z - t/\sqrt{LC})$ has $I = V/Z_0$. At the load, $V_+ + V_- = Z_L(V_+ - V_-)/Z_0$, so $\frac{V_-}{V_+} = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0}$: a
matched load absorbs everything, an open end ($Z_L = \infty$) reflects with the same sign, a short with the opposite sign; for the coaxial cable $LC = \varepsilon\mu$ (@exr-emx-wg-coax).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Hydrogen gas has an index of refraction and scatters light. The ninth exercise combines the oscillator model, the index and Rayleigh scattering.

::: {#exr-emc-hydrogen-gas}
#### Optics of atomic hydrogen

Model atomic hydrogen by one oscillator with $\hbar\omega_0 = 10.2\,$eV (the first ultraviolet line) and $f = 1$. With Sage, compute $n - 1$ at $500\,$nm for $n_{\text{at}} = 2.7\times
10^{25}\,$m$^{-3}$ and the Rayleigh cross-section at that wavelength.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega_0 = 1.55\times10^{16}\,$s$^{-1}$, $\omega = 3.77\times10^{15}\,$s$^{-1}$; $n - 1 = \frac{n_{\text{at}}e^2}{2\varepsilon_0m(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)} \approx 1.9\times10^{-4}$, the right order for hydrogen gas,
and $\sigma = \sigma_T\frac{\omega^4}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2} \approx 2.6\times10^{-31}\,$m$^2$:

{{< sage exr-emc-hydrogen-gas >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The ionosphere decides which radio waves travel beyond the horizon. The tenth exercise combines the plasma dispersion with geometry. The maximum usable frequency depends on the angle of incidence on the layer.

::: {#exr-emc-ionosphere}
#### Radio waves and the ionosphere

A layer of maximal plasma frequency $f_p = 9\,$MHz reflects waves at oblique incidence up to $f = f_p/\cos\theta_i$ (only the normal component of $\mathbf k$ feels the plasma). Explain why
AM and short-wave broadcasts reach beyond the horizon at night while FM at $100\,$MHz does not, and find the largest frequency reflected at $\theta_i = 80^\circ$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The normal component $k\cos\theta_i$ is reflected when $\omega\cos\theta_i < \omega_p$. At $\theta_i = 80^\circ$, $f_{\max} = 9/0.174 = 52\,$MHz, below FM frequencies, which therefore always cross the
ionosphere; lower frequencies bounce between ground and ionosphere and travel around the Earth.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A wire at high frequency, a waveguide and a cavity all lose energy through the skin of their walls. The last exercise compares the losses of a waveguide with those of a
cable.

::: {#exr-emc-guide-loss}
#### Losses of a waveguide

For the $\mathrm{TE}_{10}$ mode, the power lost per unit length in walls of surface resistance $R_s = \frac1{\sigma\delta}$ is $\frac12R_s\oint|\mathbf H_{\text{tan}}|^2d\ell$. Estimate with
@exr-emx-wg-power the attenuation length of a copper X-band guide at $10\,$GHz, taking $\oint|\mathbf H_{\text{tan}}|^2d\ell \sim (2a + 2b)\langle B_x^2 + B_z^2\rangle$, and explain why
waveguides replace cables at microwave frequencies.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The attenuation length is $\frac{\langle P\rangle}{dP/dz} \sim \frac{v_gab}{R_s(a + b)}$ in units where the wave impedance is $1$; in SI units with $R_s = 1/\sigma\delta = 0.026\,\Omega$ and $Z_0 =
377\,\Omega$, $\frac{Z_0ab}{R_s(a + b)} \approx 100\,$m in order of magnitude, much longer than a coaxial cable's few metres at $10\,$GHz, whose thin inner conductor carries high current density.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
